class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.title: Elementary Idea of Valence Bond Theory
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.topicTitle: Elementary idea of Valence Bond Theory
notes: **Valence Bond Theory (VBT):** a covalent bond forms when two atoms approach each other and their atomic orbitals overlap, with electrons pairing with opposite spins.
**Overlap condition:** greater overlap means stronger bond. Head-on overlap gives sigma ($\sigma$) bonds; sideways overlap gives pi ($\pi$) bonds.
**Sigma bond:** formed by end-to-end overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis. Free rotation is possible around a single $\sigma$ bond.

**Pi bond:** formed by sideways overlap of p-orbitals above and below the internuclear axis. Electron density is concentrated above and below the axis. Rotation is restricted because sideways overlap would break the bond.
**Bond strength order:** $\sigma$ bond is stronger than $\pi$ bond because end-on overlap is greater than sideways overlap.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.topicTitle: Hybridization involving s and p orbitals only
notes: **Hybridization:** the concept that atomic orbitals of similar energy mix to form new equivalent orbitals called hybrid orbitals, which then overlap to form bonds.
**sp hybridization:** one s + one p gives two sp orbitals, linear geometry, 180Â° bond angle. Example: $BeCl_2$, $CO_2$.
**sp$^2$ hybridization:** one s + two p gives three sp$^2$ orbitals, trigonal planar geometry, 120Â° bond angle. Example: $BF_3$, $C_2H_4$ (double bond contains one $\sigma$ and one $\pi$).
**sp$^3$ hybridization:** one s + three p gives four sp$^3$ orbitals, tetrahedral geometry, 109.5Â° bond angle. Example: $CH_4$, $C_2H_6$.
**Why hybridize:** VBT explains molecular geometry better than pure atomic orbital overlap. The hybrid orbitals point in directions that minimize electron-pair repulsion.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.title: Bond Characteristics â€” Length, Ionic Character and Dipole Moment
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.topicTitle: Bond characteristics: bond length, ionic character, dipole moment
notes: **Bond length:** the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Decreases with increasing bond order and increases with increasing atomic size.
**Bond energy:** the energy required to break one mole of bonds in the gas phase. Increases with bond order and decreases with increasing atomic size.
**Ionic character:** even in polar covalent bonds, the electron pair is not completely transferred. Percentage ionic character can be estimated from the electronegativity difference.
**Dipole moment $\mu$:** $\mu = q \times d$, where $q$ is the charge separation and $d$ is the bond length. Units: Debye (D).

**Polyatomic molecules:** the net dipole moment is the vector sum of individual bond dipoles. $CO_2$ has zero net dipole because the two C=O bond dipoles cancel; $H_2O$ has a net dipole because the bent shape prevents cancellation.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.title: Vander Waals Forces, Molecular Solids and Hydrogen Bonding
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.topicTitle: Vander Waal's force and molecular solids; hydrogen bonding and its application
notes: **Vander Waals forces:** weak intermolecular attractions including London dispersion forces (instantaneous dipoles), dipole-dipole forces (permanent dipoles), and dipole-induced dipole forces.
**London forces:** present in all molecules, strongest in large polarizable molecules. They explain why non-polar substances like $I_2$ and noble gases can condense into liquids and solids.
**Molecular solids:** held together by Vander Waals forces or hydrogen bonds. They have low melting points, are poor conductors, and are often volatile.

**Hydrogen bond:** a strong Vander Waals force between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, or F and a lone pair on N, O, or F of another molecule. Much stronger than ordinary Vander Waals forces but weaker than covalent bonds.

**Effects of hydrogen bonding:** water has unusually high boiling point, ice is less dense than liquid water, proteins and DNA have specific 3D structures, and cellulose fibres have high tensile strength.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.title: Metallic Bonding and Properties of Metallic Solids
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-bondin.topicTitle: Metallic bonding and properties of metallic solids
notes: **Electron sea model:** metal atoms release valence electrons into a common pool. The positive metal ions are held together by the electrostatic attraction to this sea of delocalized electrons.

**Properties explained:** high electrical and thermal conductivity (delocalized electrons move freely), malleability and ductility (layers of ions can slide without breaking bonds because electrons readjust), luster (free electrons absorb and re-emit light).

**Alloys:** mixtures of metals. Substitutional alloys (Cu-Ni, similar atomic sizes) and interstitial alloys (steel: C atoms in Fe interstices). Alloys are usually harder and have lower conductivity than pure metals.
**Bond strength:** metallic bond strength depends on the number of delocalized electrons per atom and the charge on the ions. Transition metals are strong because they have more valence electrons.
**Mercury exception:** Hg has a weak metallic bond because its 6s electrons are relativistically contracted and less available for bonding, making it liquid at room temperature.

questions.question: Using valence bond theory, explain the formation of sigma and pi bonds in ethene, C₂H₄. State the hybridisation of each carbon atom and the H–C–H bond angle.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Structure.**

Each carbon in C₂H₄ has 4 valence electrons; one is used in a double bond and three in single bonds, so each carbon is bonded to three other atoms. Steric number = 3, hence each carbon is **sp² hybridised**.

**Step 2 — Sigma bonds.**

Three sp² hybrids on each carbon lie in one plane at $120^\circ$ to each other. Two of them overlap with the 1s orbitals of H atoms (C–H σ bonds) and the third overlaps head-on with an sp² hybrid of the other carbon.

$$\text{Total } \sigma \text{ bonds} = 4(\text{C–H}) + 1(\text{C–C}) = 5 \ \sigma \text{ bonds}$$

**Step 3 — Pi bond.**

Each carbon retains one unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the plane. These two orbitals overlap sideways (laterally) to form one π bond.

$$\text{Total } \pi \text{ bonds} = 1$$

Hence the C=C double bond = 1 σ + 1 π. All six atoms are coplanar and $\angle \text{H–C–H} = 120^\circ$. Rotation about the C=C bond is restricted because it would break the π bond.
questions.knowledgeNote: In ethene each sp² carbon forms three σ bonds, and one unhybridised 2p orbital forms the single π bond.

questions.question: Predict the shape, hybridisation and bond angle of the following molecules using VSEPR theory: (a) PCl₅ (b) SF₆ (c) BeCl₂ (d) H₂S.
questions.solution:
**(a) PCl₅** — P has 5 valence electrons, all used in bonding; no lone pair. Steric number = 5 → **sp³d**, shape **trigonal bipyramidal**. Three equatorial bonds at $120^\circ$, axial–equatorial at $90^\circ$, axial–axial at $180^\circ$.

**(b) SF₆** — S has 6 valence electrons, all used in bonding; no lone pair. Steric number = 6 → **sp³d²**, shape **octahedral**. All adjacent bonds at $90^\circ$ and opposite pairs at $180^\circ$.

**(c) BeCl₂** — Be has only 2 valence electrons and forms 2 bonds with no lone pair. Steric number = 2 → **sp**, shape **linear**, angle $180^\circ$.

**(d) H₂S** — S has 6 valence electrons; 2 are used in bonding and 2 lone pairs remain. Steric number = 4 → approximately **sp³**, shape **bent (angular/V-shaped)**. The two lone pairs squeeze the bonds together so the angle is slightly less than the tetrahedral value, about **$92^\circ$** (compare $104.5^\circ$ in water, where O is more electronegative and the lone pairs are held closer to the nucleus).
questions.knowledgeNote: Five and six electron domains give trigonal bipyramidal (sp³d) and octahedral (sp³d²) shapes respectively.

questions.question: Using VSEPR theory, explain the shape of the ammonia molecule, its hybridisation and its bond angle. Why is its bond angle less than that of methane?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Electron domains.**

In NH₃, nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. Three are used in making three N–H σ bonds and one lone pair remains. So the steric number = 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = 4.

**Step 2 — Hybridisation and shape.**

Four electron domains require sp³ hybridisation, giving a tetrahedral arrangement of the four hybrids. Only three are bonded, so the molecular shape is **trigonal pyramidal**.

**Step 3 — Bond angle.**

A pure tetrahedral angle is $109^\circ 28'$. The lone pair occupies more space than a bond pair (lone pair–bond pair repulsion > bond pair–bond pair repulsion) and pushes the three N–H bonds closer together.

$$\angle \text{H–N–H} = 107^\circ$$

In CH₄ there are four bond pairs and no lone pair, so no such compression occurs and the angle is the full tetrahedral **$109^\circ 28'$**.
questions.knowledgeNote: NH₃ is sp³ hybridised and trigonal pyramidal; its lone pair compresses the H–N–H angle to 107°.

questions.question: Write the Lewis dot structure of CO₂. What is its molecular shape?
questions.solution:
Carbon (4 valence e⁻) forms double bonds with each oxygen (6 valence e⁻ each).

Lewis structure: O=C=O

Using VSEPR: 2 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs on C → **Linear** geometry, bond angle 180°.
questions.knowledgeNote: CO₂ is linear and non-polar despite having polar C=O bonds due to symmetry.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-equili.title: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
notes: **Law of mass action (Guldberg and Waage):** at a constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants raised to their stoichiometric coefficients.
**Equilibrium constant $K_c$:** for $aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$, $K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$. Concentrations are equilibrium concentrations in mol/L.
**Magnitude of $K_c$:** $K_c \gg 1$ means products dominate (reaction nearly complete). $K_c \ll 1$ means reactants dominate (reaction barely proceeds).
**Temperature dependence:** $K_c$ changes only with temperature. A catalyst changes the rate but not $K_c$ because it speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally.
**Units:** $K_c$ has units depending on the change in the number of moles of gas: $\Delta n = (c+d) - (a+b)$.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-equili.title: Equilibrium Constant Expression and Its Importance
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-equili.topicTitle: Expression for equilibrium constant and its importance
notes: **Writing $K_c$:** product concentrations raised to stoichiometric powers divided by reactant concentrations raised to stoichiometric powers. Pure solids and liquids are omitted.

**Predicting direction:** reaction quotient $Q_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$ using initial concentrations. If $Q_c < K_c$, reaction proceeds forward. If $Q_c > K_c$, reaction proceeds backward. If equal, system is at equilibrium.
**Importance:** $K_c$ tells you the extent of reaction at equilibrium, whether a reaction is feasible, and how conditions affect the equilibrium position.
**Relationship to $\Delta G$:** $\Delta G = -RT\ln K$. A large positive $K$ corresponds to large negative $\Delta G$, meaning the reaction is spontaneous.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-equili.title: Relationship Between Kp and Kc
notes: **Definitions:** $K_p$ uses partial pressures; $K_c$ uses molar concentrations.
**Relation:** $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n = (c+d) - (a+b)$ is the change in moles of gas.
**Special case â€” $\Delta n = 0$:** $K_p = K_c$. Examples: $H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI$, $N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO$.
**Units:** $K_p$ has units of pressure$^{\Delta n}$; $K_c$ has units of concentration$^{\Delta n}$. Thermodynamic equilibrium constants are dimensionless when activities are used.
**When to use which:** $K_p$ is convenient for gas-phase reactions where pressures are measured directly. $K_c$ is used when concentrations are known or when solids/liquids are involved.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemical-equili.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
notes: **Principle:** when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, the system shifts in the direction that tends to counteract the change and restore a new equilibrium.
**Concentration:** increasing reactant concentration shifts equilibrium forward; increasing product concentration shifts it backward.
**Pressure/volume:** for gas-phase reactions with $\Delta n \neq 0$, increasing pressure (decreasing volume) shifts toward the side with fewer gas moles. If $\Delta n = 0$, pressure has no effect.

**Temperature:** if the forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$), increasing temperature shifts equilibrium backward (endothermic direction). If endothermic forward, increasing T shifts forward.
**Catalyst:** does not shift equilibrium position; it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster.

questions.question: State Le Chatelier's principle. Predict the effect of increasing pressure on: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
questions.solution:
**Le Chatelier's principle:** If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the change.

Increasing pressure favors the side with fewer moles of gas.
Reactants: 1+3 = 4 moles; Products: 2 moles.
Equilibrium shifts **towards NH₃ (right)** — Haber's process uses high pressure for this reason.
questions.knowledgeNote: If Δn = 0, pressure change has no effect on equilibrium position.

questions.question: For the reaction $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$, $K_c = 0.5$ at a certain temperature. If $[N_2] = 1.0$ M and $[H_2] = 0.5$ M at equilibrium, calculate the equilibrium concentration of ammonia.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Write the equilibrium constant expression**

The coefficient 3 on $H_2$ becomes a cube and the coefficient 2 on $NH_3$ becomes a square:

$$K_c = \frac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3}$$

**Step 2 — Substitute the values**

$$0.5 = \frac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{1.0 \times (0.5)^3}$$

$$[\text{NH}_3]^2 = 0.5 \times 1.0 \times 0.125 = 0.0625$$

**Step 3 — Take the square root**

$$[\text{NH}_3] = \sqrt{0.0625} = 0.25 \ \text{M}$$

Hence the equilibrium concentration of ammonia is **0.25 M**. Notice that the very small value of $K_c$ is consistent with ammonia being formed only slowly at that temperature.
questions.knowledgeNote: Stoichiometric coefficients become powers in the equilibrium constant: $K_c = [NH₃]^2/([N₂][H₂]^3)$.

questions.question: For the equilibrium $N_2O_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)$, $\Delta H = +57$ kJ mol⁻¹, state and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium of: (a) increasing the pressure, (b) lowering the temperature, (c) adding more $N_2O_4$ at constant volume.
questions.solution:
By Le Chatelier's principle, a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose the imposed change.

**(a) Increasing the pressure → equilibrium shifts to the right (towards $NO_2$).**

On the left there is 1 mole of gas and on the right 2 moles. Increased pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles, so it opposes the volume decrease by converting $N_2O_4$ into $NO_2$. Here the greater number of moles is the more stable side at high pressure, so the shift is to the right.

**(b) Lowering the temperature → equilibrium shifts to the left (towards $N_2O_4$).**

The forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$), so heat behaves as a product. Cooling removes heat, and the system compensates by favouring the exothermic reverse reaction. Hence $N_2O_4$ forms and the colour lightens.

**(c) Adding $N_2O_4$ at constant volume → equilibrium shifts to the right.**

The concentration of $N_2O_4$ increases, so the system consumes some of the added $N_2O_4$ to restore the original concentrations. $K_c$ itself is unchanged, since temperature has not changed.
questions.knowledgeNote: Le Chatelier's principle: added heat or pressure is countered by a shift towards the endothermic or less gaseous side.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-me.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-me.title: General Principles of Extraction of Metals
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-me.topicTitle: General principles of extraction of metals: concentration, calcination, roasting, smelting, carbon reduction, thermite and electrochemical reduction
notes: **Concentration:** removing gangue to increase metal content. Methods: gravity separation, magnetic separation, froth flotation, leaching.
**Calcination:** heating ore in absence of air to remove volatile impurities and moisture. Carbonate ores decompose: $CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2$.
**Roasting:** heating ore in excess air to convert sulphide ores to oxides: $2ZnS + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2ZnO + 2SO_2$.
**Smelting:** reducing the oxide ore with carbon at high temperature: $ZnO + C \rightarrow Zn + CO$.
**Carbon reduction:** used for metals less reactive than carbon. Carbon acts as reducing agent because it has higher affinity for oxygen.
**Thermite:** highly exothermic reaction of metal oxide with aluminium powder: $Fe_2O_3 + 2Al \rightarrow 2Fe + Al_2O_3 + \text{heat}$. Used for welding railway tracks.
**Electrochemical reduction:** used for very reactive metals like Na, K, Al. Electrolysis of molten salts: $2NaCl \rightarrow 2Na + Cl_2$.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-me.title: Refining of Metals
notes: **Purpose:** to obtain metal of high purity by removing impurities from the crude metal obtained by reduction.
**Poling:** used for copper refining. Molten copper is stirred with green poles of wood, which reduce any oxide impurities. The hydrocarbon gases released also help remove dissolved gases.
**Electro-refining:** impure metal is made the anode and pure metal the cathode in a solution of its salt. Pure metal deposits on the cathode; impurities fall as anode mud.
**Copper electro-refining:** anode: impure Cu; cathode: pure Cu sheet; electrolyte: $CuSO_4$ + $H_2SO_4$. Impurities like Fe, Zn dissolve; Au, Ag, Pt fall as anode mud.
**Aluminium refining:** Hoopes process uses three layers: molten impure Al anode, molten cryolite electrolyte, molten pure Al cathode.

notes: **Group 1:** Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. One valence electron (ns$^1$). Extremely reactive, stored under oil to prevent reaction with air/moisture.

notes: **Quick lime ($CaO$):** produced by calcining limestone: $CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2$. Used in steel making, cement, and drying agent.
**Bleaching powder ($CaOCl_2$):** $Ca(OH)_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow CaOCl_2 + H_2O$. Used for bleaching and sterilizing water.

**Magnesia ($MgO$):** refractory material for furnace linings, antacid, insulator in electric wires.
**Epsom salt ($MgSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O$):** laxative, bath salt, fertilizer.
**Solubility trends:** hydroxides and sulphates become less soluble down group; carbonates become less soluble down group. $Be$ compounds are exceptions due to small size and high charge density.

questions.question: Explain Down's process for the extraction of sodium.
questions.solution:
**Down's process:** Electrolysis of molten NaCl (with CaCl₂ added to lower melting point from 801°C to ~600°C).

- Anode (graphite): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂↑ + 2e⁻
- Cathode (iron): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na↓
- Na metal collects under a steel bell
- CaCl₂ addition lowers melting point and increases conductivity
questions.knowledgeNote: Sodium cannot be extracted from aqueous solution because Na⁺ is harder to reduce than H₂O.

questions.question: Compare the extraction of sodium by the Downs cell with the extraction of magnesium by the electrolysis of fused magnesium chloride. Give the electrode reactions and state the physical state of each metal obtained.
questions.solution:
**Downs cell — sodium (NaCl melted with CaCl₂ at about 850 °C).**

Sodium is more reactive than magnesium, so its chloride must be reduced by electrolysis, not by carbon.

Cathode: $\text{Na}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Na}$. The working temperature of 850 °C is above the m.p. of sodium ($97.8$ °C), so **liquid sodium** floats up and is tapped through a separate pipe, away from the chlorine.

Anode: $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^-$. Chlorine gas rises and escapes; the iron diaphragm prevents it from mixing with the sodium.

$$2\text{NaCl(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{Na(l)} + \text{Cl}_2(g)$$

**Electrolysis of fused MgCl₂ (about 750 °C).**

Cathode: $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Mg}$. Magnesium melts at $650$ °C but the bath is kept hotter, so **solid magnesium** is deposited and scraped off, protecting it from further oxidation.

Anode: $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^-$.

$$\text{MgCl}_2(l) \rightarrow \text{Mg(s)} + \text{Cl}_2(g)$$

**Contrast.** Both need electrolysis of a fused (anhydrous) halide and both yield chlorine at the anode, but sodium is obtained as a liquid (higher operating temperature) whereas magnesium is obtained as a solid (lower operating temperature).
questions.knowledgeNote: Both metals are extracted by electrolysis of fused chlorides; sodium comes off liquid, magnesium as a solid.

questions.question: Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by carbon reduction of its oxide but is obtained by the electrolysis of a solution of alumina in molten cryolite. Give the relevant electrode reactions.
questions.solution:
**Why carbon reduction fails.**

The Gibbs energy of formation of $Al_2O_3$ is very negative (about $-1580$ kJ mol⁻¹), so aluminium is far below carbon in the Ellingham diagram. Carbon is not strong enough to reduce it, and any attempt needs temperatures at which the oxide itself would melt and decompose.

**The Hall–Héroult cell.**

Alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite, $Na_3AlF_6$ (with $CaF_2$ as a flux). Cryolite lowers the fusion temperature from about $2072$ °C to about $950$ °C and improves conductivity, so much less heat is needed and molten aluminium (m.p. $660$ °C) is tapped off as liquid.

**Cathode (carbon lining) — reduction:**

$$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Al(l)}$$

**Anode (graphite rods) — oxidation of oxide ions, the carbon burns away:**

$$\text{C} + 2\text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 4e^-$$

**Overall:**

$$2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} \rightarrow 4\text{Al} + 3\text{CO}_2$$
questions.knowledgeNote: Aluminium's oxide is too stable for carbon reduction, so Hall–Héroult electrolysis in molten cryolite is used instead.

confusion: ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ force on moving charge f = q(v×b); on a wire f = bil sinθ..
❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.
❌ Atomic number equals mass number. ✅ Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons.
❌ Bohr model explains all atoms. ✅ Bohr model works only for hydrogen-like (one-electron) systems.
❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

Quantum numbers fully describe electron state; Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund guide electron configuration.

Heisenberg uncertainty is a fundamental limit, not measurement error.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.title: Oxygen â€” Allotropes, Oxides and Applications
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.topicTitle: Allotropes of oxygen: definition of allotropy and examples; oxygen â€” types of oxides; applications of hydrogen peroxide; medical and industrial application of oxygen
notes: **Allotropy:** the existence of an element in two or more different physical forms with the same chemical composition.
**Oxygen allotropes:** dioxygen ($O_2$, stable, colourless), ozone ($O_3$, unstable, pale blue, pungent smell). Ozone is a much stronger oxidising agent than oxygen.
**Oxide types:** acidic ($SO_2$, $CO_2$), basic ($CaO$, $Na_2O$), neutral ($CO$, $N_2O$), amphoteric ($Al_2O_3$, $ZnO$), peroxide ($Na_2O_2$, $H_2O_2$), mixed oxide ($Pb_3O_4 = 2PbO \cdot PbO_2$).
**Hydrogen peroxide:** weak acid, strong oxidising and reducing agent. Decomposes: $2H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2$. Used as antiseptic, bleach, and in rocket propulsion.
**Oxygen applications:** medical (respiration therapy, anaesthesia), industrial (steel making, welding, water treatment), rocket oxidiser.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.title: Nitrogen â€” Inertness, Active Nitrogen and Ammonia
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.topicTitle: Nitrogen: reason for inertness of nitrogen and active nitrogen; chemical properties of ammonia and applications and harmful effects of ammonia
notes: **Inertness:** $N_2$ has a very strong triple bond (946 kJ/mol) and no dipole moment, making it chemically unreactive at ordinary conditions.
**Active nitrogen:** produced by passing an electric discharge through $N_2$. It is an allotrope containing atomic nitrogen and excited molecules, extremely reactive.
**Ammonia preparation:** Haber process: $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$, $\Delta H = -92.4\,\text{kJ}$. High pressure (200 atm), moderate temperature (450Â°C), iron catalyst with promoters.
**Ammonia properties:** pungent gas, highly soluble in water forming weak base $NH_4OH$. Reacts with acids to form ammonium salts, with $CuSO_4$ to give deep blue complex, with $Na$ to form sodamide.
**Applications:** fertilizers (urea, ammonium nitrate), refrigerants, cleaning agents, explosives. Harmful effects: toxic if inhaled, caustic burns, contributes to eutrophication in waterways.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.title: Nitric Acid and Halogens
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.topicTitle: Oxy-acids of nitrogen (name and formula); chemical properties of nitric acid; ring test for nitrate ion; halogens: general characteristics; comparative study of Cl2, Br2, I2; haloacids
notes: **Nitric acid preparation:** $3NaNO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow NaHSO_4 + HNO_3$ ( laboratory ). Ostwald process industrially: $4NH_3 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 4NO + 6H_2O$, then $2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2$, then $3NO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HNO_3 + NO$.

**Properties of $HNO_3$:** strong acid, powerful oxidising agent. With metals: $Cu + 4HNO_3 \rightarrow Cu(NO_3)_2 + 2NO_2 + 2H_2O$ (concentrated); $3Cu + 8HNO_3 \rightarrow 3Cu(NO_3)_2 + 2NO + 4H_2O$ (dilute). Non-metals like C and S are oxidised to $CO_2$ and $H_2SO_4$.

**Ring test for nitrate:** add $FeSO_4$ then conc. $H_2SO_4$ carefully down the side. A brown ring at the interface confirms nitrate: $NO_3^- + 3Fe^{2+} + 4H^+ \rightarrow NO + 3Fe^{3+} + 2H_2O$; $NO + Fe^{2+} \rightarrow [Fe(NO)]^{2+}$ (brown).
**Halogen trend:** reactivity decreases down group: $F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2$. Bond dissociation energy decreases down group.
**Haloacids strength:** acid strength increases down group: $HF < HCl < HBr < HI$. Bond strength decreases down group, making proton donation easier.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.topicTitle: Ozone layer depletion: causes, effects and control measures
notes: Non-metals: electronegative, form anions.
Halogen reactivity decreases down group.
Nitrogen: N₂ triple bond, very stable.
Oxygen: O₂ paramagnetic, supports combustion.
confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

Biomolecules and cell biology: Living organisms built from four macromolecule classes; cell theory unifies all life; membrane structure enables compartmentalization.

Cell division: Mitosis maintains chromosome number for growth/repair; meiosis halves it for gamete formation; crossing over creates genetic diversity.

Evolutionary biology: Darwin's natural selection explains adaptation; fossil, morphological, and molecular evidence support common ancestry; human evolution from hominid ancestors.

Floral diversity: Plant evolution from simple algae to complex angiosperms; five-kingdom classification; double fertilization unique to flowering plants.

Faunal diversity: Animal kingdom spans from unicellular protists to complex chordates; segmentation and body cavities key evolutionary innovations; earthworm and frog as model organisms.

Biota and environment: Aquatic, terrestrial, and aerial adaptations reflect evolutionary pressures; pollution from human activities threatens ecosystem stability.

Conservation biology: Biodiversity exists at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels; Nepal's protected areas and community forestry demonstrate effective conservation strategies.

Introduction to biology: Biology studies life from molecules to ecosystems; scientific method drives discovery; interdisciplinary connections with physics, chemistry, and earth science.

Introductory microbiology: Bacteria (prokaryotes) and viruses (acellular) are foundational to life sciences; Gram stain differentiates bacteria; biotechnology applications transform medicine and industry.

Vegetation: Nepal's altitude-dependent vegetation zones reflect climate gradients; in-situ (protected areas) and ex-situ (seed banks) conservation preserve plant diversity.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.title: Carbon — Allotropes and Carbon Monoxide
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.topicTitle: Carbon: allotropes of carbon (crystalline and amorphous) including fullerenes; properties and uses of carbon monoxide
notes: **Crystalline allotropes:** diamond (each C sp3 tetrahedral, hardest natural substance, insulator, high refractive index), graphite (sp2 hexagonal layers, conductor along layers, lubricant), graphene (single layer of graphite, exceptional strength and conductivity).
**Amorphous allotropes:** charcoal (activated charcoal adsorbs gases), coke (fuel in blast furnaces), lamp black (pigment and filler in inks and tyres).
**Fullerenes:** $C_{60}$ (buckminsterfullerene, football shape), $C_{70}$, nanotubes. Discovered 1985. Spherical or tubular carbon molecules with unique electronic and mechanical properties.

**Carbon monoxide:** formed by incomplete combustion. Reducing agent: $Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2$. Toxic because it binds haemoglobin 210 times more strongly than oxygen, causing asphyxiation.
**Uses of CO:** reducing agent in metallurgy, component of water gas ($CO + H_2$), feedstock for methanol and acetic acid synthesis.

class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.title: Phosphorus and Sulphur
class-11-notes/chemistry/chemistry-of-no.topicTitle: Phosphorus: allotropes; phosphine: preparation, properties and uses; sulphur: allotropes and uses; hydrogen sulphide: preparation, properties and uses; sulphur dioxide: properties and uses; sulphuric acid: properties and uses
notes: **Phosphorus allotropes:** white P (waxy, poisonous, $P_4$ tetrahedron, glows in dark), red P (amorphous, stable, non-toxic), black P (layered, conductor, most stable).

**Phosphine ($PH_3$):** prepared by reacting calcium phosphide with acid: $Ca_3P_2 + 6HCl \rightarrow 3CaCl_2 + 2PH_3$. Toxic, flammable, basic (turns red litmus blue), reducing agent (turns $CuSO_4$ solution brown).
**Sulphur allotropes:** rhombic ($S_8$ rings, stable below 95.5°C), monoclinic (stable 95.5-119°C), plastic (long chains, elastic).

**$H_2S$:** weak acid, strong reducing agent, poisonous rotten egg smell. Prepared by Kipp's apparatus: $FeS + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2S$. Forms black precipitate with lead acetate: $Pb(CH_3COO)_2 + H_2S \rightarrow PbS + 2CH_3COOH$.
**$SO_2$:** acidic, reducing (turns acidified $K_2Cr_2O_7$ from orange to green), oxidising (with $H_2S$), bleaching agent (temporary, restores colour on standing).
**$H_2SO_4$ (conc.):** dehydrating agent (chars sugar), oxidising (with Cu: $Cu + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + SO_2 + 2H_2O$), non-volatile (used to prepare volatile acids).

questions.question: Arrange the oxoacids of chlorine HClO, HClO₂, HClO₃ and HClO₄ in order of increasing acid strength and explain the trend. ($K_a$: 3.0 × 10⁻⁸, 4.0 × 10⁻², 5 × 10¹, 10¹⁰)
questions.solution:
**Order of increasing acid strength:**

$$\text{HClO} < \text{HClO}_2 < \text{HClO}_3 < \text{HClO}_4$$

This matches the increase in $K_a$ from $3.0 \times 10^{-8}$ to $10^{10}$.

**Explanation.**

Each extra oxygen atom pulls electrons away from the O–H bond through its strong $-I$ inductive effect, so the O–H bond becomes weaker and the proton is lost more easily. The $O^-$ groups generated are also stabilised by resonance delocalisation over several oxygens, making the conjugate base more stable and the acid stronger.

Pauling's empirical rule, $pK_a \approx 8 - 5m$ where $m$ is the number of non-protonated oxygen atoms, confirms it: HClO ($m=0$) gives $pK_a \approx 8$; HClO₂ ($m=1$) $pK_a \approx 3$; HClO₃ ($m=2$) $pK_a \approx -2$; HClO₄ ($m=3$) $pK_a \approx -7$. Perchloric acid is thus one of the strongest acids known.
questions.knowledgeNote: Acid strength of oxoacids rises with each added oxygen because of the inductive effect and resonance stabilisation of the anion.

questions.question: Why is helium used in diving equipment instead of nitrogen?
questions.solution: Helium is less soluble in blood than nitrogen. Under high pressure, nitrogen dissolves in blood causing 'the bends' (decompression sickness). Helium's low solubility prevents this — divers use helium-oxygen mixtures.
questions.knowledgeNote: Helium is also used in deep-sea diving because it doesn't cause nitrogen narcosis.

questions.question: Write the structure and properties of ozone (O₃).
questions.solution:
**Structure:** Bent molecule, bond angle 116.8°, bond length 128 pm. Resonance between two structures: O=O-O ↔ O-O=O.

**Properties:**
- Strong oxidizing agent
- Bleaches organic dyes
- Used in water purification
- Dissipates in sunlight: 2O₃ → 3O₂
questions.knowledgeNote: Ozone layer absorbs harmful UV radiation. CFCs destroy ozone: CFCl₃ + UV → Cl· + ...; Cl· + O₃ → ClO· + O₂

questions.question: Describe the industrial preparation of nitric acid by the Ostwald process. Give balanced equations, the catalyst and the conditions used at each stage.
questions.solution:
**Stage 1 — Oxidation of ammonia (about 850 °C, finely divided platinum or platinum–rhodium gauze).**

$$4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow[\sim 850 \ ^\circ\text{C}]{\text{Pt}} 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Stage 2 — Oxidation of nitric oxide to nitrogen dioxide (about 50 °C, fast reaction, no catalyst needed).**

$$2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO}_2$$

**Stage 3 — Absorption of nitrogen dioxide in water.**

$$3\text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{HNO}_3 + \text{NO}$$

The nitric oxide formed again is re-oxidised to $NO_2$ and re-absorbed, so nearly all the nitrogen is converted to nitric acid. The overall reaction is

$$\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

The plant is cooled continuously because the reactions are strongly exothermic.
questions.knowledgeNote: Ostwald process: ammonia is oxidised over Pt at 850 °C, NO is oxidised to NO₂, then absorbed in water to give nitric acid.

class-11-notes/chemistry/classification-.topicTitle: Modern periodic law and modern periodic table
notes: **Modern periodic law (Moseley, 1913):** the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
**Why atomic number, not mass:** Moseley showed that X-ray frequencies depend on atomic number, not atomic mass. Argon (Z=18, A=40) and potassium (Z=19, A=39) are in the correct order by Z, not A.
**Periodic table layout:** 7 periods and 18 groups. Period number equals the principal quantum number of the valence shell. Group number relates to valence electron count for main-group elements.
**Blocks:** s-block (Groups 1-2), p-block (Groups 13-18), d-block (transition metals, Groups 3-12), f-block (lanthanides and actinides, placed below main table).
**Periodicity:** elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same valence electron configuration.

class-11-notes/chemistry/classification-.title: Classification into Groups, Periods and Blocks (s, p, d, f Blocks & Metal Classifications)
class-11-notes/chemistry/classification-.topicTitle: Classification of elements into different groups, periods and blocks: s, p, d, f blocks; Metals, Non-metals, Metalloids, Coinage metals, Volatile metals
notes: ### 1. Structural Architecture of the Modern Periodic Table (Bohr's Long Form)
• Based on Moseley's Modern Periodic Law: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers (nuclear charge, Z).
• Consists of 7 horizontal rows called **Periods** and 18 vertical columns called **Groups** (IUPAC 1 to 18).
• **Period 1:** 2 elements (H, He) — shortest period (fills 1s subshell).
• **Periods 2 & 3:** 8 elements each (Li–Ne, Na–Ar) — short periods (fill 2s, 2p and 3s, 3p subshells).
• **Periods 4 & 5:** 18 elements each (K–Kr, Rb–Xe) — long periods (fill 4s, 3d, 4p and 5s, 4d, 5p subshells).
• **Period 6:** 32 elements (Cs–Rn, including 14 Lanthanides from ₅₈Ce to ₇₁Lu) — very long period (fills 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p).
• **Period 7:** 32 elements (Fr–Og, including 14 Actinides from ₉₀Th to ₁₀₃Lr) — complete radioactive period (fills 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p).
### 2. s-Block Elements (Groups 1 & 2)
• **Definition:** Elements in which the differentiating (last) electron enters the outermost s-orbital.
• **General Valence Electronic Configuration:** ns¹⁻² (Group 1 Alkali metals: ns¹; Group 2 Alkaline earth metals: ns²; where n = 2 to 7).
• **Group 1 (Alkali Metals):** ₃Li, ₁₁Na, ₁₉K, ₃₇Rb, ₅₅Cs, ₈₇Fr. Soft, silvery-white metals, highly electropositive, lowest ionization enthalpies in their periods.
• **Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals):** ₄Be, ₁₂Mg, ₂₀Ca, ₃₈Sr, ₅₆Ba, ₈₈Ra. Harder than alkali metals, +2 fixed oxidation state, basic oxides (except amphoteric BeO).

• **Key Physical Characteristics:** Low melting and boiling points due to weak metallic bonding (only 1 or 2 valence electrons in bonding sea). Densities are very low (Li, Na, K float on or displace water).

• **Flame Test:** Readily excited s-electrons emit signature colors: Li (Crimson), Na (Golden Yellow), K (Lilac/Violet), Rb (Red-Violet), Cs (Sky Blue), Ca (Brick Red), Sr (Crimson), Ba (Apple Green). Note: Be and Mg do NOT give flame coloration because their electrons are held tightly by high effective nuclear charge.

• **Chemical Properties:** Extremely strong reducing agents (standard reduction potentials: Li is most negative at -3.04 V due to exceptionally high hydration enthalpy: ΔH_hyd of Li⁺). React vigorously with water to liberate H₂: 2M + 2H₂O → 2M⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂↑.
• **Ammoniated Electrons:** Dissolve in anhydrous liquid ammonia to yield deep blue, electrically conductive, paramagnetic solutions: M + (x+y)NH₃ → [M(NH₃)_x]⁺ + [e(NH₃)_y]⁻.
• **Diagonal Relationship:** Li resembles Mg, and Be resembles Al due to similar ionic charge/radius ratio (polarizing power) and nearly identical electronegativities.
### 3. p-Block Elements (Groups 13 to 18)
• **Definition:** Elements in which the differentiating electron enters any of the three degenerate outermost p-orbitals.
• **General Valence Electronic Configuration:** ns² np¹⁻⁶ (He: 1s² is placed in Group 18 due to its filled shell noble gas behavior).

• **Families:** Group 13 (Boron family: ns² np¹), Group 14 (Carbon family: ns² np²), Group 15 (Pnictogens: ns² np³), Group 16 (Chalcogens: ns² np⁴), Group 17 (Halogens: ns² np⁵), Group 18 (Noble/Inert Gases: ns² np⁶).

• **Uniqueness:** Only block containing all three categories of matter: Metals (e.g., Al, Ga, In, Tl, Sn, Pb, Bi), Metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po), and Non-metals (C, N, O, F, Ne, P, S, Cl, Ar, Se, Br, Kr, I, Xe, Rn).

• **Inert Pair Effect:** Reluctance of the valence s-electrons to participate in chemical bonding in heavier elements of post-transition p-block elements due to ineffective shielding of intervening d and f electrons. Consequence: Lower oxidation states become progressively more stable down the group: Tl⁺ > Tl³⁺, Pb²⁺ > Pb⁴⁺, Bi³⁺ > Bi⁵⁺. Hence, PbO₂ and PbCl₄ act as strong oxidizing agents.

• **Catenation & Multiple Bonding:** Carbon shows the highest catenation power due to strong C–C single bond strength (348 kJ/mol). Second-row p-elements readily form stable pπ–pπ multiple bonds (C=C, C≡C, N≡N, C=O), whereas heavier analogues form weaker dπ–pπ or dπ–dπ bonds.

• **Anomalous Behavior of 2nd Period Elements (B, C, N, O, F):** Small atomic radii, high electronegativity, absence of vacant d-orbitals in valence shell (maximum covalency strictly limited to 4, cannot form hypervalent species like SF₆ or PCl₅).
### 4. d-Block Elements (Transition Metals, Groups 3 to 12)
• **Definition:** Elements in which the differentiating electron enters the penultimate (n-1)d subshell.
• **General Valence Electronic Configuration:** (n-1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻² (where n = 4, 5, 6, 7).
• **Four Transition Series:** 3d-series (₂₁Sc to ₃₀Zn), 4d-series (₃₉Y to ₄₈Cd), 5d-series (₅₇La, ₇₂Hf to ₈₀Hg), 6d-series (incomplete/actinoid-linked).

• **True vs Non-Typical Transition Elements:** A transition element is defined as an element having a partially filled d-orbital in its elemental ground state or in any of its common oxidation states. Zinc (₃₀Zn), Cadmium (₄₈Cd), and Mercury (₈₀Hg) have completely filled d-orbitals in elemental ground state (d¹⁰ s²) and in their +2 oxidation state (d¹⁰). Hence, they are non-typical or pseudo-transition elements.

• **Variable Oxidation States:** Due to minimal energy difference between (n-1)d and ns electrons, both sets participate in bonding. Manganese (Mn) exhibits maximum oxidation states in 3d series from +2 to +7 (e.g., KMnO₄). Osmium (Os) and Ruthenium (Ru) reach +8 (OsO₄).

• **Color of Transition Metal Ions:** Due to d-d electronic transitions. Degenerate d-orbitals split in presence of ligand fields into lower t₂g and upper eg levels. Absorption of visible light promotes electrons: Cu²⁺ (3d⁹, blue), Fe³⁺ (3d⁵, yellow/brown), Cr³⁺ (3d³, green), Ni²⁺ (3d⁸, green). Ions with d⁰ (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺) or d¹⁰ (Zn²⁺, Cu⁺, Ag⁺) are colorless.

• **Magnetic Properties:** Due to unpaired electrons. Magnetic moment calculated via spin-only formula: μ = √(n(n + 2)) Bohr Magnetons (BM), where n = number of unpaired electrons. Max in 3d is Fe³⁺ / Mn²⁺ (n = 5, μ = 5.92 BM).

• **Catalytic Properties:** High surface area and ability to adopt multiple oxidation states to form unstable reaction intermediates (e.g., Finely divided Fe in Haber process, V₂O₅ in Contact process for H₂SO₄, Ni in alkene hydrogenation, Pt in Ostwald process).

• **Interstitial Compounds & Alloys:** Small non-metal atoms (H, C, N, B) lodge into interstitial voids of metallic lattices (e.g., Steel, TiC, Fe₃H), imparting extreme hardness, high melting points, and chemical inertness.
### 5. f-Block Elements (Inner Transition Elements)
• **Definition:** Elements in which the differentiating electron enters the anti-penultimate (n-2)f subshell.
• **General Valence Electronic Configuration:** (n-2)f¹⁻¹⁴ (n-1)d⁰⁻¹ ns² (where n = 6 for 4f Lanthanides, n = 7 for 5f Actinides).
• **Lanthanide Series (4f):** 14 elements from Cerium (₅₈Ce) to Lutetium (₇₁Lu). Preceded by Lanthanum (₅₇La).
• **Actinide Series (5f):** 14 elements from Thorium (₉₀Th) to Lawrencium (₁₀₃Lr). Preceded by Actinium (₈₉Ac).

• **Oxidation States:** +3 is the universal, predominant, and most thermodynamically stable oxidation state for all Lanthanides. Some show +2 or +4 when achieving f⁰, f⁷, or f¹⁴ stable subshells (e.g., Ce⁴⁺ is 4f⁰, Eu²⁺ is 4f⁷, Yb²⁺ is 4f¹⁴). Actinides show wider range (+3, +4, +5, +6, +7) because 5f, 6d, and 7s have comparable energy levels.

• **Lanthanide Contraction (Crucial NEB Exam Concept):** Steady and progressive decrease in atomic and ionic radii (Ln³⁺) from La to Lu. Cause: Highly diffuse shape and poor screening/shielding power of 4f electrons, allowing nuclear charge (Z) to pull the outer 6s shell inward.
• **Consequences of Lanthanide Contraction:**
1. Identical radii of 4d and 5d pairs: Zr (160 pm) ≈ Hf (159 pm), Nb (146 pm) ≈ Ta (146 pm), Mo ≈ W. They occur together in nature and are extremely difficult to separate chemically.

2. Decrease in basic strength of hydroxides: As size shrinks from La³⁺ to Lu³⁺, covalent character of Ln–OH bond increases (Fajans' Rule). Thus, La(OH)₃ is the most basic, and Lu(OH)₃ is the least basic (most amphoteric).
3. Gradual increase in ionization energy, electronegativity, and electrode potential across the series.
• **Actinides Character:** All are radioactive. Beyond Uranium (Z > 92) are synthetic man-made transuranic elements.
### 6. Special High-Yield Classes of Elements in NEB Syllabus
• **Coinage Metals (Group 11 / IB):** Copper (₂₉Cu), Silver (₄₇Ag), Gold (₇₉Au).
- Possess anomalous ground state configuration: (n-1)d¹⁰ ns¹ (extra stability of fully filled d-subshell).
- Chemically inert, high positive reduction potentials (Cu: +0.34 V, Ag: +0.80 V, Au: +1.50 V). Resist oxidation by atmospheric O₂ and non-oxidizing acids (HCl, dilute H₂SO₄).
- Dissolve in oxidizing acids: Cu + 4HNO₃ (conc) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂↑ + 2H₂O.
- Gold dissolves only in Aqua Regia (3 parts conc. HCl : 1 part conc. HNO₃): Au + HNO₃ + 4HCl → H[AuCl₄] + NO↑ + 2H₂O.
- Unmatched electrical and thermal conductivity: Ag > Cu > Au.
- Form stable complexes: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (Tollens' reagent for aldehyde detection), [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ (Schweizer's reagent for dissolving cellulose).
• **Volatile Metals (Group 12 / IIB):** Zinc (₃₀Zn), Cadmium (₄₈Cd), Mercury (₈₀Hg).
- Electronic configuration: (n-1)d¹⁰ ns². Completely filled d-orbitals in both atomic and ionic (+2) states.

- Melting & Boiling points: Unusually low because paired electrons cannot participate in metallic lattice bonding. Hg is the only liquid metal at standard room temperature (MP: -38.8°C; BP: 356.7°C). Relativistic contraction pulls 6s electrons close to the nucleus, rendering them inert.

- Distinct from typical transition metals: Show only +2 oxidation state (never variable valency, except Hg which forms mercurous dimer [Hg–Hg]²⁺). Their compounds (ZnSO₄, CdCl₂, HgCl₂) are diamagnetic and white/colorless (no d-d transitions).

- Amalgams: Mercury forms liquid or solid alloys called amalgams with nearly all metals (e.g., Sodium amalgam Na-Hg, Zinc amalgam Zn-Hg used in Clemmensen reduction). Exceptions: Iron (Fe), Platinum (Pt), and Tungsten (W) do not form amalgams and are used as storage containers.
### 7. Comprehensive Classification: Metals vs Non-Metals vs Metalloids

• **Metals (~78% of elements):** Electropositive elements with low ionization enthalpies (1–3 valence electrons). Form giant metallic crystal lattices with delocalized electron gas. Form basic oxides (e.g., Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH). Good conductors, malleable, ductile, high sonority.

• **Non-Metals (18 elements total):** Electronegative elements with high ionization enthalpies and electron affinities (4–7 valence electrons, plus noble gases). High electronegativity. Form covalent or molecular lattices. Form acidic oxides (SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄) or neutral oxides (CO, NO, N₂O). Electrical insulators (except graphite).
• **Metalloids (Semimetals — B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po):** Borderline elements situated along the diagonal dividing line between metals and non-metals in the p-block.
- Possess intermediate electrical conductivity that increases with rising temperature (semiconductors, negative temperature coefficient of resistance).
- Form amphoteric or weakly acidic oxides (e.g., As₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AsCl₃ + 3H₂O; As₂O₃ + 6NaOH → 2Na₃AsO₃ + 3H₂O).

- Doping: Silicon and Germanium are doped with Group 13 elements (B, Ga) to create p-type semiconductors, or Group 15 elements (P, As) to create n-type semiconductors, forming p-n junctions for solar cells and microprocessors.
confusion: ❌ All transition elements are d-block, and all d-block elements are transition elements. ✅ All transition elements belong to d-block, but Zn, Cd, and Hg are d-block elements that are NOT transition elements because their d-subshell is completely filled (d¹⁰) in ground state and common +2 oxidation state.

❌ Hydrogen is an alkali metal because it sits in Group 1. ✅ Hydrogen has an 1s¹ configuration but is a non-metal with high ionization enthalpy (1312 kJ/mol), forming covalent bonds and H⁻ hydride ions.

❌ Helium belongs to p-block because it sits in Group 18. ✅ Helium has the valence configuration 1s² (s-block), but is placed in Group 18 above p-block noble gases due to its completely filled valence shell and inert noble chemical properties.

❌ Fluorine has the highest electron gain enthalpy (electron affinity) in the periodic table. ✅ Chlorine (Cl) has higher negative electron gain enthalpy than Fluorine (-349 kJ/mol vs -328 kJ/mol) because Fluorine's 2p subshell is very small and compact, causing strong inter-electronic repulsions that hinder incoming electrons.

❌ Ionization enthalpy always increases monotonically across a period from left to right. ✅ Exceptions exist: Beryllium (1s² 2s²) has higher IE₁ than Boron (1s² 2s² 2p¹) because 2s electrons penetrate closer to the nucleus and are fully paired; Nitrogen (2s² 2p³) has higher IE₁ than Oxygen (2s² 2p⁴) due to the extra stability of half-filled p-orbitals.
❌ Lanthanum (₅₇La) and Actinium (₈₉Ac) are f-block elements. ✅ La and Ac are d-block elements (outer configuration 5d¹ 6s² and 6d¹ 7s²). The f-block begins with Cerium (₅₈Ce) and Thorium (₉₀Th).

❌ Lanthanide contraction means the atoms expand down the group. ✅ Contraction means atomic/ionic radii decrease steadily across the 4f series from Ce to Lu due to poor shielding by diffuse 4f orbitals.

❌ Copper, Silver, and Gold are non-transition metals because their ground state is d¹⁰. ✅ They are transition metals because their common oxidation states have partially filled d-orbitals: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, Au³⁺ is 5d⁸.
❌ Graphite is an insulator like other non-metals. ✅ Graphite conducts electricity along its hexagonal sheets due to free delocalized π-electrons resulting from sp² hybridization.
❌ All oxides of metals are basic. ✅ Most are basic, but metal oxides with high oxidation states are acidic (e.g., CrO₃ with Cr⁶⁺, Mn₂O₇ with Mn⁷⁺), and some are amphoteric (Al₂O₃, ZnO, PbO, SnO).
❌ Coinage metals include Zinc, Cadmium, and Mercury. ✅ Coinage metals are strictly Group 11 (Cu, Ag, Au). Group 12 (Zn, Cd, Hg) are Volatile Metals.
❌ Mercury dissolves all metals to form amalgams. ✅ Mercury does NOT amalgamate with Iron (Fe), Platinum (Pt), or Tungsten (W); therefore, mercury is safely shipped and stored in iron flasks.

class-11-notes/chemistry/classification-.title: IUPAC Classification of Elements
notes: ### 1. Meaning — what IUPAC is and what it decides

IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) is the world authority that standardises chemical nomenclature, atomic weights and the format of the periodic table. Its classification of elements covers group numbering 1–18, the s/p/d/f block division, the metal–nonmetal–metalloid grouping, collective group names, and the naming of newly discovered elements.
### 2. IUPAC group numbering and collective names
• 18 groups numbered left to right and 7 periods; the old European (IA, IIA, … IB) and American (IA, IB, … VIIIA) systems were replaced by 1–18 to remove ambiguity.

• Collective names: Group 1 alkali metals (Li–Fr, H excluded), Group 2 alkaline earth metals (Be–Ra), Group 15 pnictogens (N–Bi), Group 16 chalcogens (O–Po), Group 17 halogens (F–At), Group 18 noble gases (He–Rn).
• Blocks: s-block (Groups 1–2 plus He), p-block (Groups 13–18 except He), d-block (Groups 3–12, transition metals), f-block (lanthanides 58–71 and actinides 90–103, inner transition metals).
### 3. IUPAC naming of new elements (Z > 100)

Discoverers propose a name and a two-letter symbol after independent verification. Until approval, a systematic name is built from digit roots — 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn — joined in order with the suffix '-ium' (temporary three-letter symbols). Examples: 104 unnilquadium (Unq) → Rutherfordium (Rf); 113 ununtrium → Nihonium (Nh); 114 ununquadium → Flerovium (Fl); 115 → Moscovium (Mc); 116 ununhexium → Livermorium (Lv); 117 ununseptium → Tennessine (Ts); 118 ununoctium (Uuo) → Oganesson (Og).
### 4. Classification by physical and chemical character
• **Metals:** the majority (s-, d-, f-blocks and lower p-block) — lustre, malleability, conductivity, basic oxides.
• **Non-metals:** upper right of the p-block (C, N, O, F, P, S, Cl, Se, Br, I, noble gases) — acidic oxides, poor conductors.
• **Metalloids (semi-metals):** B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te (sometimes Po) — intermediate properties; the basis of semiconductors.
• **Representative (typical) elements:** s- and p-blocks; **transition elements:** d-block (variable oxidation states, coloured ions, catalysts); **inner transition:** f-block.
### 5. Applications
• One agreed numbering and block scheme makes international communication and literature searching unambiguous.

• Predicting chemistry from group position: Group 1 metals are strong reducing agents, Group 17 halogens strong oxidising agents, Group 18 inert; oxide character changes from basic to acidic across a period (Na₂O, MgO basic → Al₂O₃ amphoteric → SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃ acidic).

• Standard atomic weights (from terrestrial isotopic abundance) and systematic naming keep trade, industry and metrology consistent — for example in specifying semiconductor-grade silicon or alloy composition.
• The naming and verification procedure for superheavy elements is a direct product of this classification work.
### 6. Limitations

IUPAC classification is a labelling and standardisation scheme, not an explanation — it does not say *why* properties repeat (that needs Z_eff, quantum numbers and electronic configuration). Some boundaries are arbitrary: the metal–non-metal change is gradual and metalloid membership differs between sources; H sits in Group 1 yet resembles the halogens; He is a Group 18 noble gas with the s-block configuration 1s². The composition of Group 3 for periods 6 and 7 (La/Ac versus Lu/Lr) has been debated for decades, and the '-ium' systematic names are stopgaps, so older books still print them. The chemistry of elements with Z > 103 is largely predicted, not measured.

class-11-notes/chemistry/classification-.title: Periodic Trend and Periodicity: Radii, Ionization Energy, Electron Affinity, Electronegativity, Metallic Character
class-11-notes/chemistry/classification-.topicTitle: Periodic trend and periodicity: atomic radii, ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic characters (general trend and explanation only)
notes: ### 1. Meaning of periodicity

Periodicity is the recurrence of similar physical and chemical properties at regular intervals when elements are arranged in order of atomic number. Its cause is the periodic repetition of the *valence-shell electronic configuration*: trends across a period follow from increasing Z_eff, trends down a group from increasing n and increasing shielding.
### 2. Atomic radii

Radius is measured as covalent radius (half the bond length in a homonuclear molecule), metallic radius (half the distance between neighbouring metal atoms) or van der Waals radius (from non-bonded contacts — the largest). **Across a period the radius decreases** (Li 152 → F 64 pm) because nuclear charge rises faster than shielding; **down a group it increases** (Li → Cs) because a new shell is added. Period 4 shows a normal contraction after the d-block, and the 5d series follows the 4d series closely — the lanthanide contraction (poor 4f shielding).
### 3. Ionic radii
• A cation is smaller than its parent atom (Na 186 pm → Na⁺ 95 pm); an anion is larger (Cl 99 pm → Cl⁻ 181 pm) because added electrons increase repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged.
• Down a group the ionic radius increases for the same charge (Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ < Rb⁺ < Cs⁺); across a period ions of the same charge get smaller.
• **Isoelectronic series** (same number of electrons): radius decreases as nuclear charge increases, N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Ne > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺; for one element Fe³⁺ < Fe²⁺.
### 4. Ionisation energy (IE)

The minimum energy needed to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom; measured in kJ mol⁻¹ or eV per atom (H: 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ = 13.6 eV). **It increases across a period** (Li 520 → Ne 2081 kJ mol⁻¹) because Z_eff rises and size falls, and **decreases down a group** as size increases. Anomalies: Be > B and N > O (2s² stability; 2p pairing repulsion in oxygen), repeated as Mg > Al and P > S. Successive IEs always increase (IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃), and a large jump marks the end of a shell — Na IE₁ = 496, IE₂ = 4562 kJ mol⁻¹.
### 5. Electron affinity (EA)

The energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron, X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g); EA is often reported as the energy *released*, so state the sign convention in answers. It generally becomes more exothermic **across a period** and less so **down a group** as size and shielding increase. Chlorine has a higher EA than fluorine (349 vs 328 kJ mol⁻¹) because F's very small 2p shell causes extra electron–electron repulsion. Noble gases have ~zero or positive EA, and Be and N have very small values because of filled/half-filled stability.
### 6. Electronegativity (EN)

The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared electron pair. Pauling's scale takes F = 4.0 (highest), O = 3.5, N = 3.0, H = 2.1, Cs ≈ 0.7; the Mulliken scale uses (IE + EA)/2. **EN increases across a period and decreases down a group**; noble gases are assigned little or no value. Bond polarity follows from ΔEN: > 1.7 usually ionic, < 0.5 essentially non-polar covalent (HF, ΔEN = 1.9, is polar covalent).
### 7. Metallic and non-metallic character

Metallic character **decreases across a period** (Na → Cl) and **increases down a group** (Li → Cs): metals lose electrons easily (low IE), non-metals gain them (high IE, high EA/EN). Consequences: oxide character moves from basic → amphoteric → acidic across a period, and the diagonal pairs (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) show metallic character reappearing diagonally.
### 8. Applications
• Reactivity predictions: alkali metals become more reactive down the group (low IE); halogen oxidising power falls from F to I (high EA/EN mainly for F and Cl).
• Explains the acidic/basic character of oxides, the amphoteric behaviour of Al₂O₃ and the change from ionic NaCl to covalent AlCl₃ across period 3.
• Used in materials selection (semiconductors Si, Ge), in predicting bond polarity and dipole moments, and in understanding ion sizes for crystal packing and complex formation.
### 9. Limitations of the trends

All the trends are *general*, not exact: the Be/B, N/O, Mg/Al and P/S breaks come from penetration and pairing, and the d- and f-blocks show many irregularities (Cr, Cu, lanthanide contraction, poor 4f shielding, relativistic effects in heavy elements). Radii are not directly measurable and covalent, metallic and van der Waals values differ by 0.5–1 Å, so only one consistent type may be compared. Electron affinity depends on the stated convention, and electronegativity values differ between scales (Pauling, Mulliken, Allred–Rochow), with noble-gas values ill-defined. Above all, trends are qualitative — quantitative prediction needs quantum calculations or Z_eff with accurate shielding.
confusion: ❌ Atomic radius increases across a period. ✅ It decreases because Z_eff rises faster than shielding.
❌ An anion is smaller than its parent atom. ✅ It is larger — added electrons increase repulsion while nuclear charge stays the same.
❌ IE increases smoothly across a period. ✅ Be > B and N > O (also Mg > Al, P > S) are standard breaks from 2s² stability and 2p pairing.
❌ Fluorine has the highest electron affinity. ✅ Chlorine does (349 vs 328 kJ mol⁻¹) because of extra repulsion in F's tiny 2p shell.
❌ Electronegativity is directly measurable. ✅ It is a derived, scale-dependent parameter (Pauling, Mulliken, Allred–Rochow).

questions.question: Identify the elements with atomic numbers 19, 20, 31, 36 and 55, and state the period and group in which each one is placed in the long form of the periodic table.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Number of electrons and period.**

The period number equals the number of electron shells (principal quantum number) occupied, i.e. the $n$ value of the outermost electron.

**Step 2 — Group number.**

For elements of $s$- and $p$-blocks, group number $= (number of valence electrons) + 10$.

| $Z$ | Element | Electronic configuration (outer part) | Period | Group |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 19 | Potassium (K) | $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^1$ | 4 | 1 |
| 20 | Calcium (Ca) | $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2$ | 4 | 2 |
| 31 | Gallium (Ga) | $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^24p^1$ | 4 | 13 |
| 36 | Krypton (Kr) | $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^24p^6$ | 4 | 18 |
| 55 | Caesium (Cs) | $[\text{Xe}]\,6s^1$ | 6 | 1 |

Notice that four of the five elements lie in period 4, whereas caesium (Z = 55) lies in period 6, showing that period length is not fixed.
questions.knowledgeNote: Period number equals the principal quantum number of the outermost electron, while group is decided by the valence electrons.

questions.question: Explain the following periodic irregularities: (a) the first ionisation enthalpy of Mg is greater than that of Al although Mg is to the left of Al. (b) The atomic radius of Na is greater than that of Cl.
questions.solution:
**(a) $I_1(\text{Mg}) > I_1(\text{Al})$**

$$\text{Mg}: [\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 \qquad \text{Al}: [\text{Ne}]\,3s^24p^1$$

The first electron removed from Mg comes from a completely filled $3s$ subshell, which is a particularly stable arrangement. In Al the first electron is the $3p$ electron, which is higher in energy, is shielded by the $3s$ pair and is repelled less. Since Mg's valence electron is more tightly held, $I_1(\text{Mg}) = 596$ kJ mol⁻¹ and $I_1(\text{Al}) = 578$ kJ mol⁻¹.

**(b) $r(\text{Na}) > r(\text{Cl})$**

Na and Cl are in the same period, so the number of shells is the same (n = 3). Across a period the nuclear charge increases from Na (Z = 11) to Cl (Z = 17) while the added electrons go into the same shell, so effective nuclear charge per electron rises. The stronger pull draws the cloud closer, so the radius falls.

$$r(\text{Na}) = 186 \ \text{pm} > r(\text{Cl}) = 99 \ \text{pm}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: A filled s subshell is extra stable, so Mg resists ionisation more than the higher 3p electron of aluminium.
