questions.question: A straight line passes through the point $(1,3)$ and cuts off an intercept of 7 units from the x-axis. Find its equation. Hence find the perpendicular distance of the point $(2,-1)$ from this line.
questions.solution:
An intercept of 7 on the x-axis means the line passes through $(7,0)$.

**Slope:**
$$m=\frac{3-0}{1-7}=\frac{3}{-6}=-\frac{1}{2}$$

**Equation** using $(7,0)$:
$$y-0=-\frac{1}{2}(x-7)\implies 2y=-x+7$$
$$\boxed{x+2y-7=0}$$

**Perpendicular distance** of $(2,-1)$ from $x+2y-7=0$:
$$d=\frac{|1(2)+2(-1)-7|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}}}=\frac{|2-2-7|}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{7}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{5}\approx 3.13$$

(Check the line: $(1,3)\to 1+6-7=0$ and $(7,0)\to 7-7=0$.)
questions.knowledgeNote: Distance from $(x_{1},y_{1})$ to $Ax+By+C=0$ is $\frac{|Ax_{1}+By_{1}+C|}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}$.

questions.question: Find the coordinates of the vertices and foci, the eccentricity and the length of the latus rectum of the hyperbola $9x^{2}-16y^{2}=144$.
questions.solution:
Divide throughout by 144 and put in standard form:
$$\frac{x^{2}}{16}-\frac{y^{2}}{9}=1$$
Comparing with $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$, we have $a^{2}=16,\; b^{2}=9$, so $a=4,\; b=3$.

**Vertices:** $(\pm a, 0)=(\pm 4, 0)$

**Foci:** $c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=16+9=25 \implies c=5$, so foci are $(\pm 5, 0)$.

**Eccentricity:**
$$e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{5}{4}=1.25$$

**Length of latus rectum:**
$$\frac{2b^{2}}{a}=\frac{2\times 9}{4}=\frac{9}{2}=4.5\text{ units}$$

class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.title: Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs …
class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.topicTitle: Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs of discontinuous function
notes: **Fact.** Indeterminate forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞ → L'Hôpital: lim f/g = lim f'/g' (when applicable).
**Fact.** Standard limits: lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1; lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e; lim_{x→∞} (1 + a/x)^x = e^a.
**Fact.** Continuity: f continuous at c iff lim_{x→c}f(x) = f(c). Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite.

**Removable discontinuity (hole):** The limit $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, but either $f(a)$ is undefined or $f(a) \neq \lim_{x \to a} f(x)$. The graph has a "hole" at $x = a$. Example: $f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ at $x = 1$.

**Jump discontinuity:** The left-hand and right-hand limits both exist but are not equal: $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$. The graph "jumps" at $x = a$. Example: the floor function $f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor$ at every integer.
**Infinite discontinuity (asymptotic):** At least one of the one-sided limits is $\pm \infty$. The graph has a vertical asymptote at $x = a$. Example: $f(x) = 1/x$ at $x = 0$.
**Essential (oscillatory) discontinuity:** The function oscillates infinitely near the point, so the limit does not exist in any sense. Example: $f(x) = \sin(1/x)$ at $x = 0$.
**Removable discontinuity fix:** If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ but $f(a) \neq L$ or is undefined, define a new function $g(x) = f(x)$ for $x \neq a$ and $g(a) = L$. Then $g$ is continuous at $a$.
**Graph sketching tips for discontinuous functions:** Mark open circles (holes) at removable discontinuities, closed dots at defined points, and draw vertical dashed lines at vertical asymptotes.
**Definition:** A function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = a$ if all three conditions hold: (i) $f(a)$ is defined, (ii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, (iii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$.
**Informally:** A function is continuous at a point if you can draw its graph through that point without lifting your pencil.
**Continuity on an interval:** $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous at every point in $(a, b)$, right-continuous at $a$, and left-continuous at $b$.
**Continuity of standard functions:** All polynomial, rational (where defined), trigonometric (where defined), exponential, and logarithmic functions are continuous on their domains.
**Algebra of continuous functions:** If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $x = a$, then $f + g$, $f - g$, $f \cdot g$, and $f/g$ (if $g(a) \neq 0$) are all continuous at $x = a$.
**Composition of continuous functions:** If $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(a)$, then the composite function $f \circ g$ is continuous at $a$.
**Intermediate Value Theorem:** If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a) \neq f(b)$, then $f$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ at least once on $[a, b]$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.title: Continuity of Function
notes: **The three conditions:** $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ if (i) $f(a)$ is DEFINED, (ii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ EXISTS, and (iii) the two are EQUAL. All three are required, and naming which one fails is exactly how discontinuity is classified.

**Intuitively:** the graph has no hole, no jump and no break at $a$ — it can be drawn without lifting the pencil. Since this is a limit statement, a function can be continuous everywhere yet fail to be differentiable at a corner (the case $|x|$ at 0).
**Elementary functions:** polynomials are continuous everywhere, so $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)=P(a)$ by direct substitution. $\frac1x$, $\tan x$, roots and logarithms are continuous only where defined.
**Continuity of a piece:** the test is $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=f(a)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$. For piece-wise functions this value-matches-both-sides check is almost always what a question intends.
**Removable discontinuity:** the limit exists but $f(a)$ is undefined or differs from it. Assigning the missing value equal to the limit repairs the function — a strong hint the break is removable.

**Composite and inverse:** $g\circ f$ is continuous wherever $f$ is continuous and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$; the inverse of a continuous one-to-one function is continuous on its range, which is why $\sqrt{\tan x}$ is continuous exactly where both parts are.
confusion: Checking only that $f(a)$ is defined and declaring continuity — the limit must exist and match.
Conflating continuity with differentiability — $|x|$ at 0 is continuous but not differentiable.
Using a one-sided limit in place of the two-sided one at a join point.
universalFacts: The intermediate value theorem — a continuous function on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ — is why a graph with a hole can skip a root but a graph with a jump cannot.
Physical laws are modelled as continuous because the world is, to measurement precision, free of instantaneous jumps; discontinuities in models are usually deliberate idealisations.
formulas: Composite: $g\circ f$ continuous if $f$ is and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$
keyPoints: All three conditions must hold; the failing one names the type of discontinuity.
Continuity does not imply differentiability — $|x|$ at 0 proves it.
Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions except where the denominator vanishes.

numericals:
**1. [Idea: a parameter must make the limit finite, and the point must then be defined]** Find all $a$ for which $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2+ax+3}{x-1}$ has a removable discontinuity at $x = 1$, and give the repaired value.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** For the limit to be finite the numerator must also vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $1 + a + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow a = -4$.
ewline
ewline**Check:** with $a=-4$, $x^2-4x+3 = (x-1)(x-3)$, so $f(x)=x-3$ for $x
e1$, giving $\lim_{x	o1}f = -2$.
ewline
ewline$f(1)$ is still undefined, but the break is removable: assign $f(1)=-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a=-4$, repaired value $f(1)=-2$. **Trap:** cancelling the denominator makes the limit finite, but the function is not continuous until the point itself is defined.

**2. [Idea: fewer equations than unknowns — parameterise the family]** The function $f(x)=\dfrac{ax^2+bx+c}{x-1}$ has a finite limit at $x=1$ equal to 2. Find $a,b,c$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Finite limit requires the numerator to vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $a+b+c=0 \quad (i)$.
ewline
ewlineThe removable value equals the derivative ratio, set equal to 2:$^{ ullet}$ $2a+b = 2 \quad (ii)$.
ewline
ewlineTwo equations in three unknowns — the question is deliberately **under-determined**. From (ii) $b=2-2a$; from (i) $c=-a-b = a-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a$ arbitrary, $b=2-2a$, $c=a-2$. **Check with $a=1$:** $\dfrac{x^2+3}{x-1}$, and $\lim_{x	o1} rac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=2$. ✓ **Lesson:** recognising under-determination and giving a one-parameter family is the skill tested.

**3. [Idea: exhibit both one-sided limits rather than assert them]** Show that $f(x)=\dfrac{2^{1/x}-1}{2^{-1/x}+1}$ has no limit as $x 	o 0$, and classify the discontinuity.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Put $u = 1/x$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^+$: $u	o+\infty$**, so $2^u 	o \infty$. Divide numerator and denominator by $2^u$:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0^+}\dfrac{2^u-1}{2^{-u}+1} = \lim\dfrac{1-2^{-u}}{2^{-u}+1} = \dfrac{1-0}{0+1} = 1$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^-$: $u	o-\infty$**, so $2^u 	o 0$. Numerator $	o -1$, denominator $	o 2$, giving $- rac12$.
ewline
ewlineThe one-sided limits are $1$ and $- rac12$ — both finite but UNEQUAL.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** no limit; a **JUMP** discontinuity of size $\left|1+ rac12ight| =  rac32$.

**4. [Idea: the derivative test resolves $0/0$ at any point where the numerator also vanishes]** Classify the discontinuity of $g(x)=\dfrac{\sin(\pi x)}{x(x-1)}$ at $x=0$ and at $x=1$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** The form is $ rac00$ at both, so apply the ratio-of-derivatives test.$^{ ullet}$ **At 0:** $\lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{\pi}{1} = \pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(0)=\pi$.$^{ ullet}$ **At 1:** $\lim_{x	o1}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{-\pi}{1} = -\pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(1)=-\pi$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** removable at both, repaired values $\pi$ and $-\pi$. **Note:** the test succeeds at both points only because $\sin(\pi x)$ vanishes at BOTH $0$ and $1$; had it vanished at 0 but not 1, $x=1$ would have been an infinite discontinuity.

**5. [Idea: compose the two limit statements, and notice where the hypothesis is used]** $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $g$ is continuous on $[c,d]$, and $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$. Prove $g\circ f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Fix $x_0\in[a,b]$.$^{ ullet}$ $f$ continuous at $x_0$: $\lim_{x	o x_0}f(x)=f(x_0)$.$^{ ullet}$ $f(x_0)\in[c,d]$ and $g$ continuous there: $\lim_{u	o f(x_0)}g(u)=g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewline$^{ ullet}$ As $x	o x_0$, $f(x)	o f(x_0)$, so substituting $u=f(x)$ in the second statement gives$
ewline\lim_{x	o x_0}g(f(x)) = g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewlineThat is precisely continuity of $g\circ f$ at $x_0$, and $x_0$ was arbitrary.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $g\circ f$ continuous on $[a,b]$. **Where the hypothesis matters:** the inclusion $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$ ensures the second limit is taken where $g$ is actually continuous — otherwise $f(x_0)$ could land on a hole in $g$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.title: Indeterminate Forms
notes: **What 'indeterminate' means:** a form like $0/0$ describes the SHAPE the expression takes as $x$ approaches the point, never its value. The same form can give $0$, $1$, $7$, $\infty$, or no limit at all. $\frac{x^2}{x}\to0$, $\frac{x^2}{x^2}\to1$ and $\frac{x}{x^2}\to\infty$ are all $0/0$.

**The seven forms:** $0/0$, $\infty/\infty$, $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty-\infty$, $\infty^0$, $0^0$, $1^\infty$. Everything else is determinate — $\frac{0}{5}=0$ and $\frac{5}{0}=\infty$ need no further work. $0\cdot\infty$ is the classic trap because each factor is a LIMIT rather than a value.
**Technique 1 — factorise and cancel:** find the common vanishing factor. $\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}=\lim\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=4$. For powers use $a^n-b^n=(a-b)(a^{n-1}+\dots+b^{n-1})$.

**Technique 2 — rationalise with the conjugate:** $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\lim\frac{1-\cos^2x}{x^2(1+\cos x)}=\lim\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2(1+\cos x)}=\frac12$. The conjugate is chosen so a difference of squares appears.

**Technique 3 — L'Hôpital:** for $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$, differentiate numerator and denominator SEPARATELY and take the limit of the ratio, provided that limit exists. $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ becomes $\frac{2x}{1}\to4$.
**Technique 4 — logs for $1^\infty$:** with $y=(1+f)^{g}$ and $f\to0$, take logs and use $\lim\frac{\ln(1+f)}{f}=1$, giving $\lim y = e^{\lim g\ln(1+f)}$. Hence $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac1n)^n=e$.
confusion: Reading $0/0$ as the answer — it means substitution failed, and the limit may be anything.
Applying L'Hôpital to $0\cdot\infty$ or $\infty-\infty$ without first rewriting as a quotient.
Differentiating only the numerator and forgetting the denominator.
universalFacts: Euler's number is defined as a limit, $e=\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac1n)^n$ — the compound-interest form of the $1^\infty$ case.
Numerical differentiation avoids $f(x+h)-f(x)$ over $h$ precisely because at tiny $h$ this $0/0$ suffers catastrophic cancellation.
keyPoints: An indeterminate form is a shape, not a value.
Factorise, rationalise, or use L'Hôpital — never substitute and stop.
L'Hôpital applies only to $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$.
For $1^\infty$, take logarithms to reduce to a $0/0$ quotient.
class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.summary: An indeterminate form describes the shape an expression takes near a point, never its value — the same $0/0$ may resolve to $0$, $1$, or nothing at all. specialNotes: L'Hôpital requires the derivative quotient's limit to EXIST; if it does not, the rule is silent and another technique is needed.
Some $1^\infty$ forms have no limit, so writing the form down never licenses the exponential answer.

Statement 2: L'Hôpital's rule may be applied only to $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$ forms.
Statement 3: Differentiating both parts is only part of L'Hôpital — the resulting limit must exist.
Statement 4: $0\cdot\infty$ and $\infty-\infty$ must be rewritten as a quotient first.
Statement 5: $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac{k}{n})^n = e^k$.

**1. [Idea: the denominator's limit does not exist, so the limit cannot either]** Determine $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x^2}{2x^2 + \sin^2(1/x)}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Substitute: the numerator tends to $0$ and the denominator oscillates, so the form is not even $ rac00$ and L'Hôpital is unavailable. Divide by $x^2$:$
ewline\dfrac{1}{2 + \left( rac{\sin(1/x)}{x}ight)^2}$. Put $u = 1/x$, so $u 	o \infty$ and the squared term becomes $u^2\sin^2 u$.
ewline
ewline**Examine two sequences:**$^{ ullet}$ $x_n =  rac{1}{n\pi}$ gives $\sin u = 0$, so the fraction is exactly $ rac12$.$^{ ullet}$ $y_n =  rac{1}{ rac\pi2 + 2n\pi}$ gives $|\sin u| = 1$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{1}{2+y_n^2} 	o 0$.

ewline**Answer:** DNE. **This is the concept the question tests** — students who see $ rac00$ and reach for L'Hôpital get a wrong answer.

**2. [Idea: repeated L'Hôpital, one application per order of vanishing]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x - \sin x}{x^3}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$. The numerator vanishes to **third order** because $x - \sin x$ starts with the $x^3$ term, so exactly three applications are needed.$^{ ullet}$ 1st: $\lim\dfrac{1 - \cos x}{3x^2}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 2nd: $\lim\dfrac{\sin x}{6x}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 3rd: $\lim\dfrac{\cos x}{6} =  rac16$.

ewline

ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1}{1+t^2} - 1}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1-(1+t^2)}{1+t^2}}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{-t^2}{3t^2(1+t^2)} = -\lim_{t	o0}\dfrac{1}{3(1+t^2)}$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.title: Limits of a Function
notes: **Meaning of a limit:** $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means that as $x$ gets arbitrarily close to $a$ (from either side, and without ever requiring $x = a$) the value of $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$. The point $x=a$ may be undefined and the limit still exist — which is why $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$, undefined at 2, has limit 4.

**The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition:** for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $0 < |x-a| < \delta$ implies $|f(x)-L| < \varepsilon$. The condition $0 < |x-a|$ EXCLUDES the point itself, and that exclusion is exactly what makes a limit independent of $f(a)$.

**One-sided limits:** $\lim_{x \to a^-}$ approaches from below, $\lim_{x \to a^+}$ from above. The two-sided limit exists **if and only if** both exist and are equal. Equal-but-different still means no limit — a jump discontinuity is the standard counter-example.

**Indeterminate forms are signals, not answers:** $0/0$, $\infty-\infty$, $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty/\infty$, $1^\infty$, $0^0$, $\infty^0$ mean direct substitution FAILED. Rewrite instead: factorise and cancel, rationalise with the conjugate, divide by the highest vanishing power, or use $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$.

**Infinite limits and asymptotes:** $\infty$ is never a value, only shorthand for unbounded growth. Opposite-sign one-sided limits give a VERTICAL asymptote; a finite limit at infinity gives a HORIZONTAL asymptote, found by the dominant-term rule.
confusion: Substituting the point and stopping — the limit asks what the function APPROACHES, not what it equals there.
Concluding the limit exists because both sides are 'big' — they must be the SAME FINITE number; $0/0$ or $-\infty/+\infty$ is a jump.
Writing $\lim = \infty$ as a result — a divergent limit says the function is unbounded, not that it reached a value.
universalFacts: The derivative is itself a limit, $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$, so differential calculus rests entirely on the limit concept.
A speedometer reports a limit, not an average: it is the limit of average velocities as the averaging interval shrinks to zero.
examples: Instantaneous speed: the speedometer value is a limit of average velocities taken over a shrinking interval.
Camera shutter speeds: at very short exposures the 'instant' is really an average over sensor read-out time, so a limit is only ever approached.
practiceQuestions: Q1. State the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ and explain why $0<|x-a|$ appears.
Q2. Evaluate $\lim_{x\to4}\frac{x^2-16}{x-4}$ and $\lim_{x\to5}\frac{x-2}{x-5}$, stating which is undefined at the point.
Q3. Find the horizontal and vertical asymptotes of $y=\frac{2x+1}{x^2-4}$.
keyPoints: A limit describes the value approached, not the value taken at the point.
The two-sided limit exists only if the one-sided limits are equal and finite.
$0/0$ signals failure of substitution, not a result of zero.
Infinity is never a value; it denotes unbounded growth or a vertical asymptote.
Horizontal asymptotes come from limits at infinity via the dominant-term rule.
class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.summary: A limit fixes the value a function approaches as $x$ nears $a$, independently of whether $f(a)$ is defined, which is why $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ is undefined at 2 yet has limit 4. A two-sided limit requires matching one-sided limits. Forms such as $0/0$ are not answers but signals that the function must first be rewritten by factorising, rationalising, or using $\lim\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$. Limits at infinity yield horizontal asymptotes.
specialNotes: The exclusion of $x=a$ in the epsilon-delta definition is the key subtlety: it is what makes a limit independent of the function's value at the point.
$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ holds only in radians; in degrees the value is $\frac{\pi}{180}$.
importantStatements: Statement 1: $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ does not require $f(a)$ to be defined.
Statement 2: The two-sided limit exists if and only if both one-sided limits equal the same finite number.
Statement 3: $0/0$ indicates that substitution failed, not that the limit is zero.
Statement 4: A vertical asymptote occurs where the one-sided limits diverge with opposite signs.
Statement 5: If $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L$ then $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote.
importantNotes: A limit is a boundary of behaviour, never an attained value — the same reason $f'(a)$ is independent of $f(a)$.
examShortTricks: $0/0$ fix order: factorise, rationalise (conjugate), divide by the highest vanishing power, then use $\lim\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$.
Degree check at infinity: smaller numerator degree gives 0, equal degrees gives the ratio of leading coefficients, larger gives $\pm\infty$.
Always state BOTH one-sided limits when asked about discontinuity at a point — the values carry the marks.

mcs.question: The value $f(2)$ for $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ is:
mcs.explanation: Substitution gives $0/0$, so $f(2)$ is undefined, yet $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=x+3=4$.

mcs.question: If $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=5$ and $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=5$, then $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ is:
mcs.explanation: The two-sided limit exists precisely because the one-sided limits agree.

mcs.question: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}$ with $x$ in DEGREES equals:
mcs.explanation: The standard limit equals 1 only in radians; in degrees it is $\frac{\pi}{180}\approx0.01745$.

numericals:
**1. [Idea: the denominator's limit does not exist, so the limit cannot either]** Determine $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x^2}{2x^2 + \sin^2(1/x)}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Substitute: the numerator tends to $0$ and the denominator oscillates, so the form is not even $ rac00$ and L'Hôpital is unavailable. Divide by $x^2$:$
ewline\dfrac{1}{2 + \left( rac{\sin(1/x)}{x}ight)^2}$. Put $u = 1/x$, so $u 	o \infty$ and the squared term becomes $u^2\sin^2 u$.
ewline
ewline**Examine two sequences:**$^{ ullet}$ $x_n =  rac{1}{n\pi}$ gives $\sin u = 0$, so the fraction is exactly $ rac12$.$^{ ullet}$ $y_n =  rac{1}{ rac\pi2 + 2n\pi}$ gives $|\sin u| = 1$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{1}{2+y_n^2} 	o 0$.
ewline
ewlineSince the two sequences give different values, **the limit does not exist**.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** DNE. **This is the concept the question tests** — students who see $ rac00$ and reach for L'Hôpital get a wrong answer.

**2. [Idea: repeated L'Hôpital, one application per order of vanishing]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x - \sin x}{x^3}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$. The numerator vanishes to **third order** because $x - \sin x$ starts with the $x^3$ term, so exactly three applications are needed.$^{ ullet}$ 1st: $\lim\dfrac{1 - \cos x}{3x^2}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 2nd: $\lim\dfrac{\sin x}{6x}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 3rd: $\lim\dfrac{\cos x}{6} =  rac16$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac16$. **Warning:** a fourth application would be differentiating an already non-zero limit, which is meaningless.

**3. [Idea: substitute $t = 1/x$ to convert an infinity-limit into a zero-limit]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o \infty} x^3\left(	an^{-1}\dfrac1x - \dfrac1xight)$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Naive substitution gives $\infty^3 \cdot 0$, so a change of variable is required. Let $t =  rac1x$, so $t 	o 0$ and $x^3 =  rac1{t^3}$:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{	an^{-1}t - t}{t^3}$, a $ rac00$ form.
ewline
ewlineL'Hôpital:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1}{1+t^2} - 1}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1-(1+t^2)}{1+t^2}}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{-t^2}{3t^2(1+t^2)} = -\lim_{t	o0}\dfrac{1}{3(1+t^2)}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $- rac13$. **Check:** $	an^{-1}t = t -  rac{t^3}{3} + \cdots$, so the difference is $- rac{t^3}{3}$ and multiplying by $x^3= rac1{t^3}$ indeed gives $- rac13$.

**4. [Idea: the $1^\infty$ family with a trigonometric inner function]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\left(1+\sin xight)^{ rac{1}{\sin x}}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Let $y = \left(1+\sin xight)^{1/\sin x}$ and take logarithms:$
ewline\ln y = \dfrac{\ln(1+\sin x)}{\sin x}$, which is $ rac00$.
ewline
ewlineL'Hôpital:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{ rac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}}{\cos x} = \lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x} = 1$.
ewline
ewlineSo $\ln y 	o 1$, hence $y 	o e$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $e$. **Check:** this is the general identity $\lim_{u	o0}(1+u)^{1/u}=e$ with $u = \sin x$.

**5. [Idea: the standard limit $\lim rac{e^u-1}{u}=1$ does all the work]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{2^{\sin^2 x} - 1}{x^2}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** The form is $ rac00$. Direct differentiation is circular, and a squeeze using $-x^2 \le \sin^2x \le x^2$ only bounds the expression by $ rac{2^{x^2}-1}{x^2}$, which tends to $\ln 2$ — **a non-zero bound proves nothing**.
ewline
ewlineConvert the base instead: $2^{\sin^2x} = e^{\sin^2x \ln 2}$. Set $u = \sin^2 x\,\ln 2$, so $u 	o 0$, and factor the expression into three pieces each with a known limit:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0}\underbrace{ rac{e^u-1}{u}}_{	o\,1}\cdot\underbrace{ rac{u}{\sin^2x}}_{	o\,\ln2}\cdot\underbrace{ rac{\sin^2x}{x^2}}_{	o\,1}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $1 	imes \ln 2 	imes 1 = \ln 2$. **Lesson:** when a squeeze bound tends to a non-zero constant, switch to factorisation.

**6. [Idea: chain an unknown function's limit through a rationalising identity]** Given $\lim_{x 	o 2}\dfrac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2} = 3$ and $f(2) = 6$, evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 2}\dfrac{f^2(x) - 36}{x^2-4}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$ and nothing can be computed without more information, so factor both sides:$^{ ullet}$ Numerator: $f^2(x)-36 = \left(f(x)-f(2)ight)\left(f(x)+f(2)ight)$ since $36 = f^2(2)$.$^{ ullet}$ Denominator: $x^2-4 = (x-2)(x+2)$.
ewline
ewlineThen$
ewline\lim_{x	o2}\dfrac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2}\cdot\dfrac{f(x)+f(2)}{x+2} = 3 \cdot \dfrac{6+6}{2+2} = 3 \cdot 3$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $9$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.title: Limits of a Function
notes: **Meaning of a limit:** $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means that as $x$ gets arbitrarily close to $a$ (from either side, and without ever requiring $x = a$) the value of $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$. The point $x=a$ may be undefined and the limit still exist — which is why $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$, undefined at 2, has limit 4.

**The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition:** for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $0 < |x-a| < \delta$ implies $|f(x)-L| < \varepsilon$. The condition $0 < |x-a|$ EXCLUDES the point itself, and that exclusion is exactly what makes a limit independent of $f(a)$.

**One-sided limits:** $\lim_{x \to a^-}$ approaches from below, $\lim_{x \to a^+}$ from above. The two-sided limit exists **if and only if** both exist and are equal. Equal-but-different still means no limit — a jump discontinuity is the standard counter-example.

**Indeterminate forms are signals, not answers:** $0/0$, $\infty-\infty$, $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty/\infty$, $1^\infty$, $0^0$, $\infty^0$ mean direct substitution FAILED. Rewrite instead: factorise and cancel, rationalise with the conjugate, divide by the highest vanishing power, or use $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$.

**Infinite limits and asymptotes:** $\infty$ is never a value, only shorthand for unbounded growth. Opposite-sign one-sided limits give a VERTICAL asymptote; a finite limit at infinity gives a HORIZONTAL asymptote, found by the dominant-term rule.
**Sum and difference:** if $\lim f = L$ and $\lim g = M$ then $\lim(f\pm g)=L\pm M$. Limits commute with addition because they preserve the arithmetic structure of the reals.

**Product and quotient:** $\lim(fg)=LM$ and, provided $M\ne0$, $\lim\frac{f}{g}=\frac{L}{M}$. The condition $M\ne0$ is the whole reason $0/0$ is indeterminate — the product law guarantees $0$ while the quotient law is unavailable.

**Constant multiple and power:** $\lim(cf)=cL$ and $\lim f^n=L^n$. An even root additionally needs a non-negative limit, while an odd root does not, so sign information about $L$ decides whether $\lim\sqrt[n]{f}$ exists.

**Composition:** if $\lim f=L$ and $g$ is continuous at $L$ then $\lim g(f(x))=g(L)$. This licenses substituting into a continuous outer function, and it is why a discontinuous $g$ such as $\tan$ at $\pi/2$ breaks the rule.

**Squeeze (sandwich) theorem:** if $g(x)\le f(x)\le h(x)$ near $a$ and $\lim g=\lim h=L$ then $\lim f=L$. This is the only reliable tool for a vanishing factor times an oscillating one, and it proves $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin\frac1x=0$ from $-|x|\le x\sin\frac1x\le|x|$.

**Why the laws survive discontinuity:** none of these need $f$ defined at $a$, only the limits to exist. That is exactly why a removable discontinuity does not spoil a limit, while a jump does — unequal one-sided limits mean the laws cannot be applied at all.

**The three conditions:** $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ if (i) $f(a)$ is DEFINED, (ii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ EXISTS, and (iii) the two are EQUAL. All three are required, and naming which one fails is exactly how discontinuity is classified.

**Intuitively:** the graph has no hole, no jump and no break at $a$ — it can be drawn without lifting the pencil. Since this is a limit statement, a function can be continuous everywhere yet fail to be differentiable at a corner (the case $|x|$ at 0).
**Elementary functions:** polynomials are continuous everywhere, so $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)=P(a)$ by direct substitution. $\frac1x$, $\tan x$, roots and logarithms are continuous only where defined.
**Continuity of a piece:** the test is $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=f(a)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$. For piece-wise functions this value-matches-both-sides check is almost always what a question intends.
**Removable discontinuity:** the limit exists but $f(a)$ is undefined or differs from it. Assigning the missing value equal to the limit repairs the function — a strong hint the break is removable.

**Composite and inverse:** $g\circ f$ is continuous wherever $f$ is continuous and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$; the inverse of a continuous one-to-one function is continuous on its range, which is why $\sqrt{\tan x}$ is continuous exactly where both parts are.
confusion: Substituting the point and stopping — the limit asks what the function APPROACHES, not what it equals there.
Concluding the limit exists because both sides are 'big' — they must be the SAME FINITE number; $0/0$ or $-\infty/+\infty$ is a jump.
Writing $\lim = \infty$ as a result — a divergent limit says the function is unbounded, not that it reached a value.
Using the quotient law when the denominator's limit is 0 — the law does not apply and the form is indeterminate.
Taking $\lim\sqrt{f(x)}=\sqrt{\lim f}$ without checking the sign; an even root needs a non-negative limit.
Applying the composition rule through a discontinuous outer function such as $\tan$.
Checking only that $f(a)$ is defined and declaring continuity — the limit must exist and match.
Conflating continuity with differentiability — $|x|$ at 0 is continuous but not differentiable.
Using a one-sided limit in place of the two-sided one at a join point.
universalFacts: The derivative is itself a limit, $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$, so differential calculus rests entirely on the limit concept.
A speedometer reports a limit, not an average: it is the limit of average velocities as the averaging interval shrinks to zero.
The squeeze theorem is the bridge used to prove almost every standard limit, including $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$.
Audio codecs rely on a jump discontinuity: the mapping from continuous voltage to a discrete level is a jump, and the discontinuity is audible as a click.
The intermediate value theorem — a continuous function on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ — is why a graph with a hole can skip a root but a graph with a jump cannot.
Physical laws are modelled as continuous because the world is, to measurement precision, free of instantaneous jumps; discontinuities in models are usually deliberate idealisations.
examples: Instantaneous speed: the speedometer value is a limit of average velocities taken over a shrinking interval.
Camera shutter speeds: at very short exposures the 'instant' is really an average over sensor read-out time, so a limit is only ever approached.

Squeeze: $g\le f\le h$ and $\lim g=\lim h=L \Rightarrow \lim f=L$

keyPoints: A limit describes the value approached, not the value taken at the point.
The two-sided limit exists only if the one-sided limits are equal and finite.
$0/0$ signals failure of substitution, not a result of zero.
Infinity is never a value; it denotes unbounded growth or a vertical asymptote.
Horizontal asymptotes come from limits at infinity via the dominant-term rule.
The laws need only the LIMITS to exist, not the function to be defined at the point.
The quotient law is void when the denominator's limit is 0 — the root of $0/0$.
Squeeze is the only general method for a vanishing factor times an oscillating term.
All three conditions must hold; the failing one names the type of discontinuity.
Continuity does not imply differentiability — $|x|$ at 0 proves it.
Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions except where the denominator vanishes.
class-11-notes/mathematics/calculus/conc.summary: A limit fixes the value a function approaches as $x$ nears $a$, independently of whether $f(a)$ is defined, which is why $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ is undefined at 2 yet has limit 4. A two-sided limit requires matching one-sided limits. Forms such as $0/0$ are not answers but signals that the function must first be rewritten by factorising, rationalising, or using $\lim\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$. Limits at infinity yield horizontal asymptotes. The algebraic limit laws cover sums, products, quotients, powers and composition, and each requires only that the individual limits exist — never that the functions be defined at the point. The quotient law fails precisely when the denominator tends to 0, which is why $0/0$ is indeterminate. When neither substitution nor the laws apply, the squeeze theorem settles a vanishing factor times an oscillating one. Continuity at $a$ requires three things at once: $f(a)$ defined, the two-sided limit existing, and the two being equal. Polynomials and elementary functions are continuous on their domains and composite functions inherit continuity from their parts. Continuity is strictly weaker than differentiability, which is why $|x|$ is continuous but not differentiable at 0.

mcs.question: $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin\frac1x$ is best evaluated using:
mcs.explanation: $\sin\frac1x$ has no limit, so the product law cannot apply. Bounding by $\pm|x|\to0$ settles it.

mcs.question: $\lim_{x\to0}\cos(\sin x)$ is found with the:
mcs.explanation: $\cos$ is continuous at $0$, so the composition law gives $\cos(\lim\sin x)=\cos0=1$.

mcs.question: At $x=0$, $f(x)=|x|$ is:
mcs.explanation: Both one-sided limits equal $f(0)=0$ so it is continuous; the left derivative $-1$ and right derivative $+1$ disagree, so no derivative exists.

mcs.question: $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ at $x=2$ fails which continuity condition?
mcs.explanation: The limit exists and equals 4; the failing condition is that $f(2)$ is not defined.

mcs.question: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, which must be true?
mcs.explanation: The extreme value theorem guarantees it attains a maximum and minimum, hence boundedness. Differentiability does not follow.

ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$ and nothing can be computed without more information, so factor both sides:$^{ ullet}$ Numerator: $f^2(x)-36 = \left(f(x)-f(2)ight)\left(f(x)+f(2)ight)$ since $36 = f^2(2)$.$^{ ullet}$ Denominator: $x^2-4 = (x-2)(x+2)$.
ewline
ewlineThen$
ewline\lim_{x	o2}\dfrac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2}\cdot\dfrac{f(x)+f(2)}{x+2} = 3 \cdot \dfrac{6+6}{2+2} = 3 \cdot 3$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $9$.

**1. [Idea: a parameter must make the limit finite, and the point must then be defined]** Find all $a$ for which $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2+ax+3}{x-1}$ has a removable discontinuity at $x = 1$, and give the repaired value.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** For the limit to be finite the numerator must also vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $1 + a + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow a = -4$.
ewline
ewline**Check:** with $a=-4$, $x^2-4x+3 = (x-1)(x-3)$, so $f(x)=x-3$ for $x
e1$, giving $\lim_{x	o1}f = -2$.
ewline
ewline$f(1)$ is still undefined, but the break is removable: assign $f(1)=-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a=-4$, repaired value $f(1)=-2$. **Trap:** cancelling the denominator makes the limit finite, but the function is not continuous until the point itself is defined.

**2. [Idea: fewer equations than unknowns — parameterise the family]** The function $f(x)=\dfrac{ax^2+bx+c}{x-1}$ has a finite limit at $x=1$ equal to 2. Find $a,b,c$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Finite limit requires the numerator to vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $a+b+c=0 \quad (i)$.
ewline
ewlineThe removable value equals the derivative ratio, set equal to 2:$^{ ullet}$ $2a+b = 2 \quad (ii)$.
ewline
ewlineTwo equations in three unknowns — the question is deliberately **under-determined**. From (ii) $b=2-2a$; from (i) $c=-a-b = a-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a$ arbitrary, $b=2-2a$, $c=a-2$. **Check with $a=1$:** $\dfrac{x^2+3}{x-1}$, and $\lim_{x	o1} rac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=2$. ✓ **Lesson:** recognising under-determination and giving a one-parameter family is the skill tested.

**3. [Idea: exhibit both one-sided limits rather than assert them]** Show that $f(x)=\dfrac{2^{1/x}-1}{2^{-1/x}+1}$ has no limit as $x 	o 0$, and classify the discontinuity.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Put $u = 1/x$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^+$: $u	o+\infty$**, so $2^u 	o \infty$. Divide numerator and denominator by $2^u$:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0^+}\dfrac{2^u-1}{2^{-u}+1} = \lim\dfrac{1-2^{-u}}{2^{-u}+1} = \dfrac{1-0}{0+1} = 1$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^-$: $u	o-\infty$**, so $2^u 	o 0$. Numerator $	o -1$, denominator $	o 2$, giving $- rac12$.
ewline
ewlineThe one-sided limits are $1$ and $- rac12$ — both finite but UNEQUAL.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** no limit; a **JUMP** discontinuity of size $\left|1+ rac12ight| =  rac32$.

**4. [Idea: the derivative test resolves $0/0$ at any point where the numerator also vanishes]** Classify the discontinuity of $g(x)=\dfrac{\sin(\pi x)}{x(x-1)}$ at $x=0$ and at $x=1$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** The form is $ rac00$ at both, so apply the ratio-of-derivatives test.$^{ ullet}$ **At 0:** $\lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{\pi}{1} = \pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(0)=\pi$.$^{ ullet}$ **At 1:** $\lim_{x	o1}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{-\pi}{1} = -\pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(1)=-\pi$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** removable at both, repaired values $\pi$ and $-\pi$. **Note:** the test succeeds at both points only because $\sin(\pi x)$ vanishes at BOTH $0$ and $1$; had it vanished at 0 but not 1, $x=1$ would have been an infinite discontinuity.

**5. [Idea: compose the two limit statements, and notice where the hypothesis is used]** $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $g$ is continuous on $[c,d]$, and $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$. Prove $g\circ f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Fix $x_0\in[a,b]$.$^{ ullet}$ $f$ continuous at $x_0$: $\lim_{x	o x_0}f(x)=f(x_0)$.$^{ ullet}$ $f(x_0)\in[c,d]$ and $g$ continuous there: $\lim_{u	o f(x_0)}g(u)=g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewline$^{ ullet}$ As $x	o x_0$, $f(x)	o f(x_0)$, so substituting $u=f(x)$ in the second statement gives$
ewline\lim_{x	o x_0}g(f(x)) = g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewlineThat is precisely continuity of $g\circ f$ at $x_0$, and $x_0$ was arbitrary.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $g\circ f$ continuous on $[a,b]$. **Where the hypothesis matters:** the inclusion $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$ ensures the second limit is taken where $g$ is actually continuous — otherwise $f(x_0)$ could land on a hole in $g$.

questions.question: The curve $y=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x-2$ is given. Find (i) its stationary points, (ii) classify each of them, (iii) its point of inflection, and (iv) the equation of the tangent at the point of inflection.
questions.solution:
**(i) Stationary points:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^{2}-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)$$
Stationary at $x=1$ and $x=3$.
$$y(1)=1-6+9-2=2,\qquad y(3)=27-54+27-2=-2$$
So the stationary points are $(1,2)$ and $(3,-2)$.

**(ii) Classification:**
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=6x-12$$
At $x=1$: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-6<0\Rightarrow(1,2)$ is a **point of local maximum**.
At $x=3$: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=6>0\Rightarrow(3,-2)$ is a **point of local minimum**.

**(iii) Point of inflection:**
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=0\Longrightarrow 6x-12=0\Longrightarrow x=2,\qquad y(2)=8-24+18-2=0$$
So the point of inflection is $(2,0)$.

**(iv) Tangent at $(2,0)$:** slope $=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\Big|_{x=2}=3(2-1)(2-3)=-3$.
$$y-0=-3(x-2)\Longrightarrow\boxed{3x+y-6=0}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: For a cubic, $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=0$ gives the single inflection point, and the tangent there cuts the cubic with multiplicity 3.

questions.question:
If $y=(\sin x)^{\cos x}$, show that
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=y\left(\cos x\,\cot x-\sin x\,\log_{e}(\sin x)\right)$$
and hence find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ when $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
questions.solution:
Take logarithms of both sides:
$$\log y=\cos x\cdot\log(\sin x)$$
Differentiate (product rule):
$$\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=-\sin x\log(\sin x)+\cos x\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$$
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=y\left[\cos x\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}-\sin x\,\log(\sin x)\right]=y\left(\cos x\,\cot x-\sin x\,\log_{e}(\sin x)\right)$$

**At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:** $\sin x=\cos x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\cot x=1$, $\log_{e}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=-\tfrac12\log_{e}2$, and $y=\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^{1/\sqrt2}$.
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^{1/\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\log_{e}2\right)$$
$$\approx 0.7827\times 0.7071\times 1.3466\approx \boxed{0.745}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: Logarithmic differentiation of $u^{v}$ needs BOTH terms $v'\log u$ and $v\frac{u'}{u}$.

questions.question: Differentiate with respect to $x$: (i) $y=x^{x}$  (ii) $y=\sin^{2}x\cdot e^{x}$  (iii) $y=(1+x)^{1/x}$
questions.solution:
**(i) $y=x^{x}$** — write it in exponential form:
$$y=e^{x\log_{e}x}$$
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{x}\left(\log_{e}x+x\cdot\frac{1}{x}\right)=\boxed{x^{x}(1+\log_{e}x)}$$

**(ii) $y=\sin^{2}x\,e^{x}$** — product rule:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=2\sin x\cos x\cdot e^{x}+\sin^{2}x\cdot e^{x}=\boxed{e^{x}\sin x\left(\sin x+2\cos x\right)}$$

**(iii) $y=(1+x)^{1/x}$** — take logarithms:
$$\log y=\frac{1}{x}\log(1+x)$$
$$\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{x}\cdot\frac{1}{1+x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\log(1+x)$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=(1+x)^{1/x}\cdot\frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{1}{1+x}-\frac{\log(1+x)}{x}\right)}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: For $y=u(x)^{v(x)}$ take logs: $y'=y\left[v'\log u+v\frac{u'}{u}\right]$.

questions.question: Using the first principles of differentiation, show that $\displaystyle \frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{1/3}\right)=\frac{1}{3x^{2/3}}$. Hence find the derivative of $y=(2x+3)^{1/3}$.
questions.solution:
Let $y=x^{1/3}$. Then
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{(x+h)^{1/3}-x^{1/3}}{h}$$
Put $a=x^{1/3}$ and $b=(x+h)^{1/3}$. Then
$$b^{3}-a^{3}=h\;\Longrightarrow\;(b-a)(b^{2}+ab+a^{2})=h\;\Longrightarrow\;b-a=\frac{h}{b^{2}+ab+a^{2}}$$
$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{b^{2}+ab+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{3a^{2}}=\frac{1}{3x^{2/3}}$$

**Hence**, for $y=(2x+3)^{1/3}$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{3}(2x+3)^{-2/3}\times 2=\boxed{\frac{2}{3(2x+3)^{2/3}}}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: First principles uses $a^{3}-b^{3}=(a-b)(a^{2}+ab+b^{2})$; the increment $h$ cancels and the result follows by substitution.

questions.question: $\displaystyle \frac{d}{dx}\left[\log_{a}(\sin x)\right]$ is (a) $\frac{1}{\sin x\,\log_{e}a}$  (b) $\frac{\cot x}{\log_{e}a}$  (c) $\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$  (d) $\tan x\log a$
questions.solution:
Using $\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}\log_{a}u=\frac{u'}{u\log_{e}a}$ with $u=\sin x$, $u'=\cos x$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\log_{a}(\sin x)=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x\cdot\log_{e}a}=\frac{\cot x}{\log_{e}a}$$

**Correct option: (b)**
questions.knowledgeNote: $\frac{d}{dx}\log_{a}x=\frac{1}{x\ln a}$ — the extra $\ln a$ in the denominator is easy to forget.

class-11-notes/mathematics/computational.topicTitle: Mechanics (optional): Statics â€” forces and resultant forces, parallelogram law of forces, composition and resolution of forces, resultant of coplanar forces acting on a point; Dynamics â€” motion of particle in a straight line, motion with uniform acceleration, motion under gravity, motion down a smooth inclined plane
notes: **Parallelogram law:** if two forces $P$ and $Q$ act at a point with angle $\theta$ between them, the resultant $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$.
**Resolution:** any force can be resolved into two perpendicular components. $F_x = F\cos\theta$, $F_y = F\sin\theta$.
**Equilibrium:** for a particle, $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$. Lami's theorem for three coplanar forces in equilibrium: $\frac{P}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R}{\sin\gamma}$.
**Uniform acceleration equations:** $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
**Motion under gravity:** downward: $v = gt$, $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = 2gh$. Upward: $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
**Inclined plane:** acceleration down smooth incline: $a = g\sin\theta$. Time to reach bottom from rest: $t = \sqrt{\frac{2l}{g\sin\theta}}$, where $l$ is length of plane.

questions.question: Newton's forward difference formula is applied to tabulated equal-interval values of $y$ in order to (a) extrapolate from the beginning of the table (b) extrapolate from the end of the table (c) interpolate anywhere in the table (d) differentiate the function
questions.solution:
Newton's forward formula is
$$y(x)=y_{0}+p\Delta y_{0}+\frac{p(p-1)}{2!}\Delta^{2}y_{0}+\frac{p(p-1)(p-2)}{3!}\Delta^{3}y_{0}+\cdots,\qquad p=\frac{x-x_{0}}{h}$$
Here $y_{0}$ is the **first** value in the table and the differences are built forward from it, so the method is efficient when $x$ lies near $x_{0}$ — i.e. at the beginning of the tabulation. (For values near the end, one uses the **backward** difference formula.)

**Correct option: (a)**
questions.knowledgeNote: Newton's forward formula starts from $y_{0}$ (first tabulated value); near the end of the table use the backward formula instead.

questions.question: The displacement of a particle at time $t$ second is $s = 2t^{3}-3t^{2}+5t-4$ metre. Find (i) its velocity and acceleration when $t=2$ second, and (ii) whether the particle is ever momentarily at rest.
questions.solution:
**Velocity** is $\dfrac{ds}{dt}$ and **acceleration** is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{d^{2}s}{dt^{2}}$.

**(i)**
$$v=\frac{ds}{dt}=6t^{2}-6t+5$$
$$a=\frac{dv}{dt}=12t-6$$
At $t=2$ second:
$$v=6(4)-6(2)+5=24-12+5=17\ \text{m/s}$$
$$a=12(2)-6=18\ \text{m/s}^{2}$$

**(ii)** The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$6t^{2}-6t+5=0$$
The discriminant is
$$\Delta=(-6)^{2}-4(6)(5)=36-120=-84<0$$
There is no real root, so **the particle is never at rest**. (Confirmation: $v$ has its least value at $t=\frac{6}{2\times 6}=\frac12$, where $v=6(0.25)-3+5=3.5>0$ m/s.)
questions.knowledgeNote: If $v=0$ has a negative discriminant the particle never stops; alternatively check $v$ at the vertex of the quadratic.

questions.question: Evaluate: (i) $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x-x\cos x}{x^{3}}$  (ii) $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{x-\sin x}{x^{3}}$.
questions.solution:
**(i)** Both numerator and denominator tend to 0, so apply L'Hôpital's rule:
$$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\cos x-(\cos x-x\sin x)}{3x^{2}}=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{x\sin x}{3x^{2}}$$
$$=\frac{1}{3}\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}\cdot\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{x}=\frac{1}{3}\times 1\times 1$$
$$\boxed{\frac{1}{3}}$$

**(ii)** Applying L'Hôpital's rule three times:
$$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\cos x}{3x^{2}}=\frac{1}{3}\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2\sin^{2}\frac{x}{2}}{x^{2}}$$
$$=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\lim_{x\to 0}\left(\frac{\sin\frac{x}{2}}{\frac{x}{2}}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{2}{12}\times 1$$
$$\boxed{\frac{1}{6}}$$

(Equivalently, from the Taylor expansions $\sin x=x-\frac{x^{3}}{6}+\cdots$ and $\cos x=1-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\cdots$: $\sin x-x\cos x=\frac{x^{3}}{3}-\frac{x^{5}}{30}$ and $x-\sin x=\frac{x^{3}}{6}-\frac{x^{5}}{120}$.)
questions.knowledgeNote: Memorise $\lim\frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}}=\frac12$ and $\lim\frac{x-\sin x}{x^{3}}=\frac16$.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2-\sqrt{4-x}}{x-4}$, $x\neq 4$. (a) Show that $f(0)$ is defined. (b) Using the first principles of differentiation, find $f'(0)$. (c) Find $f'(2)$.
questions.solution:
**(a)**
$$f(0)=\frac{2-\sqrt{4}}{0-4}=\frac{2-2}{-4}=0$$
So $f(0)$ exists and equals $0$.

**(b)** By first principles,
$$f'(0)=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x-0}=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2-\sqrt{4-x}}{x(x-4)}$$
Rationalise the numerator: $(2-\sqrt{4-x})(2+\sqrt{4-x})=4-(4-x)=x$.
$$f'(0)=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{(2+\sqrt{4-x})(x-4)}=\frac{1}{(2+2)(-4)}=\boxed{-\frac{1}{16}}$$

**(c)** With $N=2-\sqrt{4-x}$ and $D=x-4$,
$$\frac{dN}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4-x}},\qquad \frac{dD}{dx}=1$$
$$f'(x)=\frac{\frac{x-4}{2\sqrt{4-x}}-\left(2-\sqrt{4-x}\right)}{(x-4)^{2}}$$
At $x=2$ ($\sqrt{2}$):
$$f'(2)=\frac{-2}{2\sqrt{2}}-2+\sqrt{2}}{4}=\frac{-\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{2}-4}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{1}=\frac{\sqrt{2}-4}{8}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: First principles needs $f(a)$ to exist; if it does, compute $f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$.

questions.question: $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{x}-1}{x}$ equals (a) 0  (b) 1  (c) $e$  (d) $\infty$
questions.solution:
The limit is of the form $\frac{0}{0}$, so apply L'Hôpital's rule:
$$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{x}-1}{x}=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{x}}{1}=e^{0}=1$$

(Equivalently, $\frac{d}{dx}e^{x}=e^{x}$ so $\frac{e^{x}-1}{x-0}$ is the slope of the chord of $y=e^{x}$ between $0$ and $x$, tending to the derivative at $0$.)

**Correct option: (b) 1**
questions.knowledgeNote: The fundamental limit $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{x}-1}{x}=1$ is the base of all standard exponential limits.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{7+x}-3}{x-2}$.
questions.solution:
Substituting $x=2$ gives $\frac{0}{0}$, so the limit is of the indeterminate form; **rationalise** the numerator with the conjugate $\sqrt{7+x}+3$.

$$\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{7+x}-3}{x-2}\times\frac{\sqrt{7+x}+3}{\sqrt{7+x}+3}$$
$$=\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{(7+x)-9}{(x-2)(\sqrt{7+x}+3)}$$
$$=\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{(x-2)(\sqrt{7+x}+3)}$$
$$=\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{7+x}+3}$$
$$=\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}+3}=\frac{1}{3+3}=\boxed{\frac{1}{6}}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: For $0/0$ limits with a radical, multiply by the conjugate so that the factor $(x-a)$ cancels.

questions.question: The variance of the first 10 natural numbers is (a) 8.25  (b) 9.25  (c) 10.25  (d) 11.25
questions.solution:
**Known result:** for the first $n$ natural numbers (i.e. $1, 2, \dots, n$) the variance is $\dfrac{n^{2}-1}{12}$.

Putting $n = 10$:
$$v = \frac{10^{2}-1}{12} = \frac{100-1}{12} = \frac{99}{12} = \frac{33}{4} = 8.25$$

(Check: mean $= \frac{1+2+\cdots+10}{10}=5.5$; the sum of squared deviations $= 247.5$, and $247.5/10 = 8.25$.)

**Correct option: (a) 8.25**
questions.knowledgeNote: For the first $n$ natural numbers, variance $=\frac{n^{2}-1}{12}$ and standard deviation $=\sqrt{\frac{n^{2}-1}{12}}$.

questions.question: If $P(A)=0.6$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.3$, then $P(A\cup B)$ is (a) 0.8  (b) 1.0  (c) 0.7  (d) 1.4
questions.solution:
By the **addition theorem** of probability,
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$$
$$P(A\cup B)=0.6+0.5-0.3=1.1-0.3=0.8$$

(The subtraction is necessary because $A\cap B$ is counted twice in $P(A)+P(B)$.)

**Correct option: (a) 0.8**
questions.knowledgeNote: Always subtract $P(A\cap B)$ when adding $P(A)+P(B)$, since the intersection is counted twice.

questions.question: A lot contains 20 items of which 3 are defective. Two items are drawn at random without replacement and both are found to be defective. Find the probability that (i) both items drawn are defective, (ii) exactly one of the two items drawn is defective, and (iii) the third item drawn next is also defective.
questions.solution:
Total items $=20$, defective $=3$, good $=17$.

**(i) Both defective:**
$$P = \frac{3}{20}\times\frac{2}{19} = \frac{6}{380} = \frac{3}{190}$$

**(ii) Exactly one defective:** (mutually exclusive ways — D then G, or G then D)
$$P = \left(\frac{3}{20}\cdot\frac{17}{19}\right)+\left(\frac{17}{20}\cdot\frac{3}{19}\right) = \frac{2\times 51}{380} = \frac{102}{380} = \frac{51}{190}$$

**(iii) Third item also defective, given the first two were defective:**
After removing 2 defectives, 18 items remain with only $1$ defective, so
$$P = \frac{1}{18}$$

**Answers:** (i) $\frac{3}{190}$  (ii) $\frac{51}{190}$  (iii) $\frac{1}{18}$
questions.knowledgeNote: Without replacement the numerators shrink as the draws proceed: $\frac{3}{20},\frac{2}{19},\frac{1}{18}$ while the denominator drops by 1 each time.

class-11-notes/mathematics/trigonometry/.title: Inverse Circular Functions
notes: **Why inverse functions are needed:** sine, cosine and tangent are periodic and many-to-one, so they do not have true inverses unless their domains are restricted.

**Principal value branches:** the restricted domains that make the functions one-to-one: $\sin^{-1}x$ on $[-1,1]$ with range $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$; $\cos^{-1}x$ on $[-1,1]$ with range $[0, \pi]$; $\tan^{-1}x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with range $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$.
**Negative argument rules:** $\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x$; $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x$; $\tan^{-1}(-x) = -\tan^{-1}x$.
**Sum formula:** $\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\right)$ when $xy < 1$.
confusion: Inverse trigonometric functions are not the same as $1/\sin x$ or $1/\cos x$. $\sin^{-1}x$ means the angle whose sine is $x$, not the reciprocal.
The range of $\sin^{-1}x$ is $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, not the full circle. Always check which branch you are in.
practice: Find the value of $\tan^{-1}(1) + \tan^{-1}(2) + \tan^{-1}(3)$.
If $\sin^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}y = \pi/2$, show that $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.
universalFacts: Inverse trigonometric functions always return principal values by convention.
The sum of complementary inverse functions (sin and cos, tan and cot) is always $\pi/2$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/trigonometry/.title: Trigonometric Equations and General Values
formulas: **Multiple & Submultiple Angles — the complete formula sheet for NEB.**
**Power & product rewiring — the bridge to submultiple angles**
$$\tan\frac{A}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos A}{1+\cos A}} = \frac{\sin A}{1+\cos A} = \frac{1-\cos A}{\sin A}$$
$$\cot\frac{A}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos A}{1-\cos A}} = \frac{\sin A}{1-\cos A} = \frac{1+\cos A}{\sin A}$$
**± rule:** in $\sin\frac A2$, $\cos\frac A2$ and $\tan\frac A2$ take $+$ or $-$ from the quadrant in which $\frac A2$ lies — $A/2$ is not automatically acute.
**Any angle $nA$ — de Moivre, the source of every formula above**
$$\left(\cos A + i\sin A\right)^n = \cos nA + i\sin nA$$

Expand the left side with the binomial theorem and match the real and imaginary parts: $\cos nA$ and $\sin nA$ fall out as polynomials in $\sin A$ and $\cos A$ — that is exactly how the 2A, 3A and 4A identities above are generated.

questions.question: If $\tan\alpha=2$ and $\tan\beta=3$, find (i) $\tan(\alpha+\beta)$, (ii) $\tan(\alpha-\beta)$, and (iii) verify your answer to (i) using $\sin(\alpha+\beta)$ and $\cos(\alpha+\beta)$.
questions.solution:
**(i)**
$$\tan(\alpha+\beta)=\frac{\tan\alpha+\tan\beta}{1-\tan\alpha\tan\beta}=\frac{2+3}{1-6}=\frac{5}{-5}=\boxed{-1}$$

**(ii)**
$$\tan(\alpha-\beta)=\frac{\tan\alpha-\tan\beta}{1+\tan\alpha\tan\beta}=\frac{2-3}{1+6}=\boxed{-\frac{1}{7}}$$

**(iii)** From $\tan\alpha=2$, take $\sin\alpha=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}$, $\cos\alpha=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}$; from $\tan\beta=3$, take $\sin\beta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}$, $\cos\beta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$.
$$\sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta=\frac{2}{\sqrt{50}}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{50}}=\frac{5}{5\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$$
$$\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{50}}-\frac{6}{\sqrt{50}}=-\frac{5}{\sqrt{50}}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$$
$$\therefore\ \tan(\alpha+\beta)=\frac{1/\sqrt2}{-1/\sqrt2}=-1$$
which agrees with part (i). Also $\sin(\alpha+\beta)>0$, $\cos(\alpha+\beta)<0$, so $\alpha+\beta$ lies in the second quadrant.
questions.knowledgeNote: When $1-\tan\alpha\tan\beta=0$ the addition formula for $\tan$ fails; find $\alpha+\beta$ from $\sin$ and $\cos$ instead.

questions.question: Solve for $x$, $0^{\circ}<x<90^{\circ}$: (i) $\displaystyle \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}+\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}=2\sqrt3$  (ii) $3\sin^{2}x-4\cos^{2}x+1=0$
questions.solution:
**(i)** Multiply the second numerator and denominator by $(1-\cos x)$:
$$\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}=\frac{\sin x(1-\cos x)}{1-\cos^{2}x}=\frac{\sin x(1-\cos x)}{\sin^{2}x}=\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}$$
So the left side becomes
$$\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}+\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}=\frac{2}{\sin x}$$
Hence $2\sin x = 2\sqrt3 \Rightarrow \sin x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, giving
$$x=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)\approx 35.264^{\circ}\approx\boxed{35^{\circ}16'\text{ (approximately)}}$$

**(ii)** Using $\sin^{2}x=1-\cos^{2}x$:
$$3(1-\cos^{2}x)-4\cos^{2}x+1=0$$
$$3-3\cos^{2}x-4\cos^{2}x+1=0\Longrightarrow 4-7\cos^{2}x=0$$
$$\cos x=\frac{2}{\sqrt7}\quad(\cos x>0\text{ on }0^{\circ}\!<x\!<90^{\circ})$$
$$x=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt7}\right)\approx\boxed{40.9^{\circ}}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: $\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}=\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}=\tan\frac{x}{2}$; their sum collapses to $\frac{2}{\sin x}$.

questions.question: $\sin^{2}30^{\circ}+\cos^{2}60^{\circ}-\tan^{2}45^{\circ}$ is (a) 1  (b) 0  (c) $\frac{1}{2}$  (d) $-\frac{1}{2}$
questions.solution:
Using $\sin30^{\circ}=\frac12$, $\cos60^{\circ}=\frac12$, $\tan45^{\circ}=1$:
$$\left(\frac12\right)^{2}+\left(\frac12\right)^{2}-1^{2}=\frac14+\frac14-1=\frac12-1=-\frac12$$

**Correct option: (d) $-\frac{1}{2}$**
questions.knowledgeNote: $\sin^{2}30^{\circ}=\cos^{2}60^{\circ}=\frac14$ and $\tan^{2}45^{\circ}=1$, which changes the sign of such expressions.

questions.question:
Prove that
$$\cos\theta+\cos3\theta+\cos5\theta+\cdots+\cos(2n-1)\theta=\frac{\sin2n\theta}{2\sin\theta}$$
questions.solution:
Multiply both sides by $2\sin\theta$ and use $2\sin A\cos B=\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)$:

$$2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta$$
$$2\sin\theta\cos3\theta=\sin4\theta-\sin2\theta$$
$$2\sin\theta\cos5\theta=\sin6\theta-\sin4\theta$$
$$\vdots$$
$$2\sin\theta\cos(2n-1)\theta=\sin2n\theta-\sin(2n-2)\theta$$

Adding all these equations, every intermediate term cancels in pairs:
$$2\sin\theta\left[\cos\theta+\cos3\theta+\cos5\theta+\cdots+\cos(2n-1)\theta\right]=\sin2n\theta$$
Dividing by $2\sin\theta$:
$$\cos\theta+\cos3\theta+\cdots+\cos(2n-1)\theta=\frac{\sin2n\theta}{2\sin\theta}$$
which is the required result.
questions.knowledgeNote: Multiply an odd cosine series by $2\sin\theta$: the terms telescope to $\sin2n\theta$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/vectors/conce.title: Vector Algebra â€” Types, Addition and Scalar Multiplication
class-11-notes/mathematics/vectors/conce.topicTitle: Scalar and vector quantities, types of vectors; addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors
notes: **Scalar vs vector:** scalars have magnitude only (mass, temperature); vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, force).

**Types of vectors:** equal vectors (same magnitude and direction), opposite vectors (same magnitude, opposite direction), unit vector (magnitude 1), null vector (magnitude 0), parallel vectors, collinear vectors, coplanar vectors.
**Addition:** $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \vec{b} + \vec{a}$ (commutative). Triangle law: place tail of $\vec{b}$ at head of $\vec{a}$; resultant closes the triangle.

**Subtraction:** $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \vec{a} + (-\vec{b})$. Geometrically, draw $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ from same point; $\vec{a} - \vec{b}$ is the vector from head of $\vec{b}$ to head of $\vec{a}$.
**Scalar multiplication:** $k\vec{a}$ has magnitude $|k|\cdot|\vec{a}|$. If $k>0$, direction unchanged; if $k<0$, direction reversed; if $k=0$, null vector.

class-11-notes/mathematics/vectors/conce.title: Dot Product and Its Applications
class-11-notes/mathematics/vectors/conce.topicTitle: Dot product (scalar product) and its applications
notes: **Definition:** $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = a_xb_x + a_yb_y + a_zb_z$.
**Geometric meaning:** measures how much two vectors align. $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|$ times projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\vec{a}$.
**Perpendicularity test:** $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$ if and only if $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$.
**Work:** $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta$. Only the component of force along displacement does work.
**Angle between vectors:** $\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/vectors/conce.title: Cross Product and Its Applications
class-11-notes/mathematics/vectors/conce.topicTitle: Cross product (vector product) and its applications
notes: **Definition:** $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta \, \hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, given by right-hand rule.
**Component form:** $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (a_yb_z - a_zb_y)\hat{i} + (a_zb_x - a_xb_z)\hat{j} + (a_xb_y - a_yb_x)\hat{k}$.
**Magnitude:** $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.
**Zero condition:** $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}$ if $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are parallel or antiparallel ($\theta = 0$ or $\pi$).
**Torque:** $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$. Angular momentum: $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Magnetic force: $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

class-11-notes/mathematics/vectors/conce.title: Scalar and Vector Triple Products
notes: **Scalar triple product:** $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$. It equals the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$.

**Properties:** $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{b} \cdot (\vec{c} \times \vec{a}) = \vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ (cyclic). If any two vectors are equal or parallel, the product is zero.
**Vector triple product:** $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})\vec{b} - (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})\vec{c}$. This expands a cross-of-cross into a linear combination.
**Applications:** scalar triple product gives volume; vector triple product appears in torque and angular momentum calculations and in simplifying vector expressions.

questions.question: The scalar projection of the vector $\mathbf{a}=(2,-1,4)$ on the vector $\mathbf{b}=(1,2,-2)$ is (a) $-\frac{8}{3}$  (b) $\frac{8}{3}$  (c) $-\frac{8}{9}$  (d) $8$
questions.solution:
Scalar projection $=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|}$.

$$\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=2(1)+(-1)(2)+4(-2)=2-2-8=-8$$
$$|\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{1+4+4}=\sqrt{9}=3$$
$$\text{Scalar projection}=\frac{-8}{3}$$

**Correct option: (a) $-\frac{8}{3}$**
questions.knowledgeNote: Scalar projection divides $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}$ by $|\mathbf{b}|$; vector projection divides it by $|\mathbf{b}|^{2}$.

questions.question: What is the scalar triple product? Write its geometric significance.
questions.solution:
The scalar triple product is [a b c] = a · (b × c).

**Geometric significance:** It gives the volume of the parallelepiped formed by vectors a, b, c.

If [a b c] = 0, the three vectors are coplanar (lie in the same plane).
questions.knowledgeNote: Scalar triple product is cyclic: [a b c] = [b c a] = [c a b]

questions.question: The position vectors of the points $A$ and $B$ are $\mathbf{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$. Find the position vector of the point which divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $2:3$.
questions.solution:
If $P$ divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $m:n$ (i.e. $AP:PB=m:n$), then
$$\mathbf{p}=\frac{n\,\mathbf{a}+m\,\mathbf{b}}{m+n}$$
Here $m=2$, $n=3$:
$$\mathbf{p}=\frac{3(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k})+2(\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k})}{5}$$
$$=\frac{(6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-3\hat{k})+(2\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+4\hat{k})}{5}$$
$$=\frac{8\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+\hat{k}}{5}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf{p}=\frac{8}{5}\hat{i}-\frac{3}{5}\hat{j}+\frac{1}{5}\hat{k}}$$

**Verification:** $\overrightarrow{AP}=\left(-\frac25,-\frac85,\frac65\right)$ and $\overrightarrow{PB}=\left(-\frac35,-\frac{12}{5},\frac95\right)$, so $|AP|^{2}=\frac{104}{25}$, $|PB|^{2}=\frac{234}{25}$ and $|AP|:|PB|=\sqrt{104:234}=2:3$.
questions.knowledgeNote: For $AP:PB=m:n$ the position vector is $\frac{n\mathbf{a}+m\mathbf{b}}{m+n}$ — the weights are swapped.

questions.question: Given $\mathbf{a}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, find (i) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}$ and (ii) $|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|$, and verify your results.
questions.solution:
**(i) Scalar product**
$$\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=1(3)+(-2)(4)+3(-1)=3-8-3=\boxed{-8}$$

**(ii) Vector product**
$$\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\ 1&-2&3\\ 3&4&-1\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=\hat{i}\big[(-2)(-1)-(3)(4)\big]-\hat{j}\big[(1)(-1)-(3)(3)\big]+\hat{k}\big[(1)(4)-(-2)(3)\big]$$
$$=\hat{i}(2-12)-\hat{j}(-1-9)+\hat{k}(4+6)=-10\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+10\hat{k}$$
$$|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{(-10)^{2}+10^{2}+10^{2}}=\sqrt{300}=\boxed{10\sqrt3}$$

**Verification:** $|\mathbf{a}|^{2}=1+4+9=14$, $|\mathbf{b}|^{2}=9+16+1=26$, so $|\mathbf{a}|^{2}|\mathbf{b}|^{2}=14\times26=364$.
$$(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})^{2}+|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|^{2}=64+300=364\ \checkmark$$
questions.knowledgeNote: Use $(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})^{2}+|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|^{2}=|\mathbf{a}|^{2}|\mathbf{b}|^{2}$ to check both parts at once.

questions.question: (i) Find a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing $\mathbf{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. (ii) Find the area of the triangle whose vertices are $A(1,1,1)$, $B(2,-1,3)$ and $C(-1,2,2)$.
questions.solution:
**(i)**
$$\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{vmatrix}=\hat{i}(1\cdot1-0\cdot1)-\hat{j}(1\cdot1-0\cdot0)+\hat{k}(1\cdot1-1\cdot0)$$
$$=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$$
$$|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt3$$
The required unit normal is
$$\hat{n}=\frac{\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{3}}$$

**(ii)**
$$\overrightarrow{AB}=(2-1,\,-1-1,\,3-1)=(1,-2,2),\qquad \overrightarrow{AC}=(-1-1,\,2-1,\,2-1)=(-2,1,1)$$
$$\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&-2&2\\-2&1&1\end{vmatrix}=\hat{i}(-2\cdot1-2\cdot1)-\hat{j}(1\cdot1-2(-2))+\hat{k}(1\cdot1-(-2)(-2))$$
$$=-4\hat{i}-5\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$$
$$|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|=\sqrt{16+25+9}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2$$
$$\text{Area of }\triangle ABC=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|=\boxed{\frac{5\sqrt2}{2}\text{ square units}}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: Area of a triangle $=\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$; the cross product gives the plane normal.

questions.question: विराम चिह्नको प्रयोग गरी निम्न वाक्यलाई शुद्ध रूपमा लेख्नुहोस्: 'हाम्रो विद्यालय काठमाडौँको तारामाथा भएको छ साथै यसको आँगनमा बेमौसम फूल फुल्छ।'
questions.solution:
**शुद्ध वाक्य:**
> हाम्रो विद्यालय काठमाडौँको तारामाथा भएको छ**,** **साथै** यसको आँगनमा बेमौसम फूल फुल्छ।

**कारण:** यो **जमिल वाक्य** हो — 'छ' पछि 'साथै' गरी दुई उपवाक्य छन्। जमिल वाक्यमा संयोजक शब्द (साथै, तर, र, किनभने) लाई **अर्धविराम ( , )** ले छुट्याइन्छ र **पूर्ण विराम ( । )** मात्र वाक्यको अन्त्यमा राखिन्छ।

संयोजक शब्द हटाई दुई स्वतन्त्र वाक्य बनाए पनि शुद्ध हुन्छ — *'हाम्रो विद्यालय काठमाडौँको तारामाथा भएको छ। यसको आँगनमा बेमौसम फूल फुल्छ।'*
questions.knowledgeNote: जमिल वाक्यमा संयोजक शब्द छुट्याएर अर्धविराम प्रयोग गरिन्छ र पूर्ण विराम मात्र अन्त्यमा राखिन्छ।

questions.question: 'शब्द' र 'वाक्य' बीच के भिन्नता छ? उदाहरण सहित वर्णन गर्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**शब्द:** कुनै पनि अर्थ बोध गर्ने सानो भाग। उदाहरण: घर, पानी, राम

**वाक्य:** एक वा अधिक शब्दले बनेको पूर्ण अर्थबोधक संरचना। उदाहरण: रामले घर बनायो।

मुख्य भिन्नता: शब्द अकेलै पूर्ण अर्थ दिन सक्दैन, वाक्यले पूर्ण अर्थ दिन्छ।
questions.knowledgeNote: शब्द = building block; वाक्य = complete meaningful expression.

questions.question: निम्नमध्ये कुन शब्द तत्पुरुष समास हो? (क) मामाचेला (ख) नेपालभाषा (ग) दशलाख (घ) चतुर्दशी
questions.solution:
**सही उत्तर: (ख) नेपालभाषा**

'नेपालभाषा' = **नेपाल + भाषा**। यहाँ द्वितीय (अधिलम्बित) पदबाट 'को' विभक्ति विलोप भई **प्रथम पद (नेपाल) मात्र प्रधान** भएकाले यो **तत्पुरुष समास** हो।

अन्य विकल्पहरू:
- **(क) मामाचेला** = मामा + चेला — दुवै पद स्वतन्त्र, अर्थपूर्ण र समान पदा भएकाले **द्वन्द्व समास** हो।
- **(ग) दशलाख** = दश + लाख — अङ्क र अङ्क जोडिएकाले **अङ्कात्मक द्विगु समास** हो।
- **(घ) चतुर्दशी** = चतुः + दशी — यो पनि अङ्क र अङ्क जोडिएकाले **अङ्कात्मक द्विगु समास** हो।
questions.knowledgeNote: तत्पुरुष समासमा द्वितीय पदको विभक्ति विलोप भई प्रथम पद मात्र प्रधान हुन्छ, जस्तै नेपालको भाषा = नेपालभाषा।

questions.question: दिइएका वचनहरूको बहुवचन रूप लेख्नुहोस्: (क) कक्षा (ख) पुस्तक (ग) घर
questions.solution:
(क) कक्षा → **कक्षालाईहरू** / कक्षाहरू
(ख) पुस्तक → **पुस्तकहरू**
(ग) घर → **घरहरू**
questions.knowledgeNote: नप्ल भाषामा बहुवचन बनाउन '-हरू' प्रत्यय जोडिन्छ।

questions.question: निम्न शब्दहरूमा उपसर्ग छुट्याई उपसर्गको नाम र शब्दको अर्थ लेख्नुहोस्: (१) प्रभार (२) प्रवास (३) अभय (४) सगति।
questions.solution:
(१) **प्रभार = प्र + भार** — उपसर्ग **'प्र'**; अर्थ — प्रतिभार गर्नु, थिच्नु; सामाजिक दबाब।
(२) **प्रवास = प्र + वास** — उपसर्ग **'प्र'**; अर्थ — परिवास गर्नु (बस्नु), अर्को देशमा बस्नु।
(३) **अभय = अ + भय** — उपसर्ग **'अ'**; अर्थ — निर्भय रहनु, सुरक्षित हुनु।
(४) **सगति = स + गति** — उपसर्ग **'स'**; अर्थ — सहगति गर्नु, साथ दिनु।

यी चारै शब्दमा उपसर्ग मूल शब्दको अर्थलाई बदलेर शब्दमा नयाँ अर्थ दिएको छ।
questions.knowledgeNote: उपसर्ग मूल शब्दको अर्थ बदल्ने शब्द-प्रयोगी तत्व हो, जस्तै 'अ + भय = अभय' भने निर्भय हुनु।

questions.question: 'एकान्तनिवास' कुन साहित्यकारको रचना हो? यो कुन विधाको संग्रह हो र यसमा कुन सामाजिक यथार्थको चित्रण गरिएको छ?
questions.solution:
'एकान्तनिवास' **नेमबहादुर हिडी** को रचना हो। यो उनको **निबन्ध संग्रह** हो — कृतिको नाम 'एकान्त + निवास' बाट बनेको हो, जसको अर्थ एकान्तमा बस्नु सङ्केतित गर्छ।

यस संग्रहका निबन्धहरूले **गाउँ र सहरको जीवनको असमानता, गरिबी, शोषण र व्यवस्थापकीय कमजोरी** जस्ता सामाजिक यथार्थको चित्रण गरेका छन्।

यहाँ देखिने प्रमुख साहित्यिक विशेषता — **व्यंग्यात्मक र आलोचनात्मक शैली**। लेखकले सामान्य जीवनका घटनाबाट गहन सामाजिक निष्कर्ष निकाल्न शैली अपनाएका छन्।
questions.knowledgeNote: नेमबहादुर हिडीको एकान्तनिवास निबन्ध संग्रहले सामाजिक असमानता र शोषणको यथार्थ चित्रण गर्छ।

questions.question: नाटक भनेको के हो? नाटकका मुख्य अङ्गहरू नाम लेख्नुहोस् र नाटक अन्य साहित्यिक विधाभन्दा भिन्न किन हुन्छ भनी स्पष्ट पार्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**नाटकको परिभाषा:** नाटक भनेको त्यस्तो साहित्यिक रचना हो जसमा पात्रहरूको **अभिनय** मार्फत घटना–क्रम अगाडि बढ्छ र जीवनयापरको यथार्थ, आचरण वा समस्या प्रस्तुत गरिन्छ।

**नाटकका मुख्य अङ्गहरू:**
1. **दृश्य (वातावरण)** — काल, स्थान, वस्तु–स्थिति र परिस्थिति बुझाउने
2. **संवाद (भाषा)** — चरित्रको भावना, सम्बन्ध र कारण प्रकट गर्ने
3. **अभिनय** — पात्रको मुख, हात, शरीर र स्वरबाट भाव प्रकट गराउने
4. **अलङ्कार**
5. **वेशभूषा**
6. **सङ्गीत**
7. **प्रवेश–निर्गमद्वार** (पात्रको प्रवेश र निर्गमको ठाउँ)

**भिन्नता:** नाटक **अभिनययोग्य** साहित्यिक विधा हो — यो मञ्चमा देखाउन मिल्ने भाषा, अङ्ग र दृश्य यसका अनिवार्य तत्त्व हुन्। कथा, कविता र निबन्ध पढ्ने वा सुन्दा मात्र बुझिने भए पनि नाटकलाई अभिनय गरेर नै यसको पूर्ण अर्थ बुझ्न सकिन्छ।
questions.knowledgeNote: नाटक अभिनययोग्य विधा हो, जसका मुख्य अङ्गमा दृश्य, संवाद, अभिनय, अलङ्कार, वेशभूषा र सङ्गीत पर्छन्।

questions.question: निम्नमध्ये लेखक र कृतिको जोडी सही कुन हो? (क) सानेपाखि — नेमबहादुर हिडी (ख) माटोको टिप्परी — टकरबहादुर राई (ग) भँडारी — अमर नेपाल (घ) रूपसू — बुद्धभक्ति आचार्य
questions.solution:
**सही उत्तर: (क) सानेपाखि — नेमबहादुर हिडी**

'सानेपाखि' नेमबहादुर हिडीको प्रसिद्ध **कथासङ्ग्रह** हो।

अन्य विकल्पका सही जोडी:
- **(ख)** माटोको टिप्परी — **रुद्रबहादुर राई** (टकरबहादुर राई होइनन्)।
- **(ग)** भँडारी — **हरिमाल** (अमर नेपाल होइनन्)।
- **(घ)** रूपसू — **सकुन्तला** (बुद्धभक्ति आचार्य होइनन्)।
questions.knowledgeNote: नेमबहादुर हिडीले सानेपाखि (कथा) र एकान्तनिवास (निबन्ध) दुई विधाकै लेखनीय कृति लेखेका छन्।

questions.question: 'विज्ञानले मानव जीवनलाई कसरी सरल र समृद्ध बनाएको छ' विषयमा निबन्धको अनुच्छेद-योजना र प्रमुख वाक्यहरू लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**निबन्धको ढाँचा: भूमिका → विषय-विस्तार → उपसंहार**

**१. भूमिका (परिचय वाक्य):**
- टोपिक वाक्य: *आज विज्ञानले हाम्रो दैनिक जीवन यत्ति नै बदलिदिएको छ कि यसलाई केवल दैनिक सुविधा भन्ने सोच पनि पर्याप्त छैन।*

**२. विषय-विस्तार (तीन उपअनुच्छेद):**
- **क) शिक्षा र सूचना प्रविधि** — टोपिक वाक्य: *अब कुनै पनि विषय कुनै पनि दिनमा, घरबाटै सिक्न सकिन्छ।* (मोबाइल, इन्टरनेट, अनलाइन कक्षा र पुस्तकालयको विस्तार)
- **ख) स्वास्थ्य र जीवनस्तर** — टोपिक वाक्य: *आजको चिकित्सा विज्ञानले असाधारण मानिसलाई पनि बाँचाउन सक्ने भएको छ।* (औषधि, शल्य चिकित्सा, खोप र सफा पानी)
- **ग) कृषि र उत्पादन तथा चुनौती** — टोपिक वाक्य: *विज्ञानले उत्पादन बढाए पनि प्रकृतिको असन्तुलन बढाउने जोखिम पनि बढाएको छ।*

**३. उपसंहार (निष्कर्षात्मक वाक्य):**
- *विज्ञान आफैँमा न त पूज्य छ न दुःखदाता; कसरी प्रयोग गर्ने भन्ने निर्णय मानिसकै हो।*

**ध्यान दिनुपर्ने कुरा:** प्रत्येक उपअनुच्छेदको पहिलो वाक्य **मुख्य भाव (topic sentence)** स्पष्ट हुनुपर्छ र उदाहरण वा कारणले समर्थित हुनुपर्छ।
questions.knowledgeNote: निबन्धमा भूमिका, विषय-विस्तार र उपसंहार यी तीन भाग अनिवार्य रूपमा हुनुपर्छ।

questions.question: 'दैनिक जीवनमा अनुशासनको महत्त्व' विषयमा ८–१० वाक्यको एउटा अनुच्छेद लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**नमूना अनुच्छेद:**

*अनुशासन* भनेको आफूलाई आद्यालमा बाँध्ने बानी हो। **[भूमिका]** दैनिक जीवनमा अनुशासनले हामीलाई काम क्रमबद्ध र अरुको समय तथा भावना प्रति सम्मान गर्न सिकाउँछ। **[विस्तार]** विद्यालयमा पढाइ ठीक समयमा सुरु गर्नु, किताब र कपडा चोखो पार्नु, गृहकार्य समयमै नै गर्नु अनुशासनकै सुरुवात हो। जो विद्यार्थी आफ्नो काममा अनुशासित छैन, उसले कक्षामा अरुलाई बाधा पुर्‍याउँछ र परीक्षामा पनि पछि पर्छ। **[विस्तार]** अनुशासनले व्यक्तिगत जीवन मात्र सुन्दर बनाउँदैन, समाजमा नैतिकता र अनुशासनको स्थापना गर्न मद्दत गर्छ। **[निष्कर्ष]** त्यसैले अनुशासनलाई जेरजरी नमानी जीवनभर सिकाइमा सधैं लागू राख्नुपर्छ।

**अनुच्छेद लेखनका आधारभूत कुरा:**
1. पहिलो वाक्यमा **मुख्य भाव (topic sentence)** स्पष्ट हुनुपर्छ।
2. बीचका वाक्यहरू उदाहरण, कारण वा तुलनाले **समर्थन** गर्नुपर्छ।
3. अन्त्यको वाक्य **निष्कर्षात्मक** हुनुपर्छ र सबै अनुच्छेद एकै भावसँग सम्बन्धित हुनुपर्छ।
questions.knowledgeNote: अनुच्छेदको पहिलो वाक्य मुख्य भाव हुनुपर्छ र अन्त्यको वाक्य निष्कर्षात्मक हुनुपर्छ।

questions.question: जिल्ला स्तरीय खेलकुद प्रतियोगिता सुरु हुँदै भएकाले विद्यालयको खेलकुद समितिका सदस्यहरूलाई भाग लिन आमन्त्रित गर्ने पत्र लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**नमूना पत्र (आमन्त्रण पत्र):**

**मिति:** २०८१/०२/१५

**प्रापक:**
श्री अध्यक्षज्यू,
खेलकुद समिति,
सत्योशी माध्यमिक विद्यालय, ................. , जिल्ला।

**विषय:** जिल्ला स्तरीय खेलकुद प्रतियोगितामा सहभागिताको लागि आमन्त्रण।

**महोदय,**

जिल्ला स्तरीय खेलकुद प्रतियोगिता सुरु हुँदै भएकाले त्यसमा हाम्रो विद्यालयको खेलकुद समितिका सदस्यहरूको सहभागिता अत्यन्त आवश्यक भएको छ। प्रतियोगिताको मिति, स्थान र खेलको विवरण यसैसाथ पठाइएको छ।

सहभागी खेलाडीहरूको नामावली र पूर्ण विवरण हाम्रो विद्यालयमा उपलब्ध छ। समयमै खेलाडी पठाइदिनुहोला भन्ने हार्दिक निवेदन छ।

धन्यवाद।

भवदीय,

नाम: .................
कक्षा: .................
विज्ञान/खेल: .................
हस्ताक्षर: .................

**पत्र लेखनका आवश्यक अङ्गहरू:** मिति, प्रापकको नाम-ठेगाना, विषय, सम्बोधन, विषयवस्तु, समापन (भवदीय) र नाम-ठेगाना-हस्ताक्षर।
questions.knowledgeNote: औपचारिक पत्रमा मिति, प्रापकको ठेगाना, विषय, सम्बोधन, विषयवस्तु र नाम-हस्ताक्षर क्रमशः अनिवार्य हुन्छन्।

class-11-notes/nepali/sahitya-adhyayan/n.title: कविता परिचय (Introduction to Poetry)
notes: कविता साहित्यको त्यस्तो विधा हो जसमा भावना, अनुभव र कल्पनालाई लय, ताल, प्रतीक र अलङ्कारका माध्यमबाट कलात्मक रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरिन्छ। कविता भनेको शब्दहरूबाट बनेको चित्र हो जसले पाठकको मनमा भावना जगाउँछ।
कविताका तत्वहरू

भावना (Emotion): कविताको प्राण भावना नै हो — प्रेम, वेदना, देशभक्ति, प्रकृतिप्रतिको आकर्षण आदि। कल्पना (Imagination): कविले कल्पनाको सहाराले वस्तु र घटनालाई नयाँ रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्छ। लय (Rhythm): शब्दहरूको आवृत्तिबाट सिर्जना हुने संगीतात्मक प्रवाह। प्रतीक (Symbol): वस्तु वा घटनाले अर्को गहिरो अर्थलाई संकेत गर्छ। अलङ्कार (Figure of speech): उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा आदिको प्रयोगले कवितालाई सुन्दर बनाउँछ।
कविताका प्रकारहरू

कविता मुख्यतया दुई प्रकारकी हुन्छन्: गद्य कविता (Free verse) जसमा नियमित लय वा तुक नहुन सक्छ, र छन्दोबद्ध कविता (Metrical poetry) जसमा निश्चित छन्द, गति र तुक हुन्छ। विषयवस्तुका आधारमा कवितालाई प्रकृति कविता, देशभक्ति कविता, प्रेम कविता, आधुनिक कविता आदिमा वर्गीकरण गर्न सकिन्छ।
NEB पाठ्यक्रममा कविता

NEB (राष्ट्रिय परीक्षा बोर्ड) को नेपाली पाठ्यक्रममा कविता अध्ययनको उद्देश्य विद्यार्थीहरूमा भावनात्मक संवेदना, भाषिक सौन्दर्यबोध र आलोचनात्मक चेतना विकास गर्नु हो। कविता पढ्दा भाव, भाषा, शिल्प र सन्देश — यी चार पक्षमा ध्यान दिनुपर्छ।
